title: Glossary
text:
Definitions of terms used throughout the website


Scope Terms specific to a single case study (programme names, voucher types) are not repeated here; they are explained on the page where they appear, for example Examples.


A

Activities The concrete actions taken to deliver a programme, such as running grant calls, disbursing subsidies or delivering advisory services. What a programme does, as distinct from its inputs or its outputs.
Additionality The share of a programme’s activity that would not have happened without it. Firms that would have invested anyway generate little that is truly additional per euro of public money spent.
Assumptions In a Theory of Change, the conditions that must hold for one step in a programme’s causal chain to lead to the next. If an assumption does not hold, for example that firms face a genuine financing constraint, a programme can produce outputs without producing real outcomes.
Attrition Participants dropping out of a study, or no longer responding to follow-up data collection. It becomes a risk when dropout is not random: if struggling firms are the ones most likely to disappear, the firms still measured make a programme look better than it is.



B

Balance How similar the treatment and comparison groups look on observable characteristics before a programme starts. A successful random assignment should produce balance; large, systematic differences are a warning sign that something went wrong with the draw.
Baseline data Data collected from participants before a programme begins, used as the starting point against which later change is measured.
Bin-ranking design An RCT design in which applicants are scored and sorted into bins: the highest scorers are funded automatically, the lowest are rejected, and only the middle bin, where expected returns are least certain, is randomised between a treatment and a comparison group. Also called a cutoff design; effective when eligibility criteria are clear and resources are limited.



C

Cohesion Policy The EU’s main investment policy for reducing economic and social disparities between regions, delivered mainly through the ERDF and the ESF+.
Common output indicator (COI) A standardised output measure that Managing Authorities report to the European Commission for ERDF and ESF+ programmes, such as the number of firms supported.
Common result indicator (CRI) A standardised result measure that ERDF and ESF+ programmes report to the European Commission, corresponding closely to a programme’s medium-term outcomes.
Community Innovation Survey (CIS) A recurring EU survey of firm-level innovation activity. One of several validated frameworks Managing Authorities can draw on when defining evaluation indicators.
Comparison / Control Group The group not receiving the intervention, used as a benchmark for what would have happened to the treatment group without it.
Confidence level How certain an evaluation needs to be that a measured effect is not simply due to chance. One of the inputs to a power calculation.
Confounding factors External characteristics (variables) that can distort the perceived relationship between a policy intervention and its outcomes, leading to incorrect conclusions about the policy’s effectiveness.
Contamination The often unintended exposure of participants in the comparison group to the randomly assigned programme, which can compromise the comparison between the two groups and affect the study’s validity.
Cost-benefit analysis Weighing a programme’s measured impact against its cost, to judge whether it was a good use of public money and to compare it with alternative investments.
Counterfactual outcome An attempt to mimic the hypothetical outcome in the scenario of what would have happened without the newly introduced change (treatment, programme, implementation approach, investment).



D

Deadweight Support that funds activity a firm would have carried out anyway. High deadweight, the mirror image of low additionality, means public money is substituting for spending the firm would have made regardless.
Difference-in-differences (DiD) A quasi-experimental method that compares the change over time in a treatment group with the change over the same period in a comparison group that had a similar prior trend. Relies on the parallel trends assumption, that both groups would have followed the same trajectory without the programme, which cannot be tested directly.
Digital Economy and Society Index (DESI) A European Commission index tracking digital performance and adoption. Used as an outcome measure in the SMART Romania case study to track firms’ digital adoption.



E

Encouragement design Randomising who receives extra outreach to take up a programme that cannot be denied to anyone, then comparing the whole encouraged group with the whole non-encouraged group. Used when take-up, not access, is the problem.
Endline data Data collected once a programme has run long enough for effects to plausibly appear, used to measure the gap between the treatment and comparison groups.
European Regional Development Fund (ERDF) An EU Cohesion Policy fund that co-finances regional programmes, including many of the business-support and innovation programmes evaluated on this site.
European Social Fund Plus (ESF+) An EU Cohesion Policy fund that co-finances programmes on employment, skills and social inclusion.



G

Goals In a Theory of Change, the long-term aspirations behind a policy, such as a more innovative regional economy or greater resilience to economic shocks. Goals typically take years to materialise.



I

Impact evaluation An assessment of whether, and by how much, a programme caused the changes observed, by comparing participants’ outcomes with a credible counterfactual. It serves two purposes: policy learning (what works, for whom, and under what conditions) and accountability (both financial and performance).
Implementation problems A risk to an RCT’s validity where the programme itself is delivered unevenly across participating firms, making the treatment experienced by the treatment group less consistent than intended.
Innovation activity All developmental, financial and commercial activities undertaken by a firm that are intended to result in an innovation.
Inputs In a Theory of Change, the resources invested in a policy: financing, personnel, equipment and training. For ERDF programmes, inputs typically include EU and national co-financing and the administrative capacity of the Managing Authority.
Intention-to-treat (ITT) effect The effect estimated by comparing groups exactly as originally assigned by randomisation, regardless of whether firms assigned to treatment actually took it up. It stays unbiased because assignment was random, but it understates the effect on firms that actually participated.
Intervention logic The account, already required for ERDF and ESF+ programmes, of how a policy instrument is expected to produce its intended results. A Theory of Change builds on this by adding explicit assumptions and showing which links in the chain are strong or uncertain.



L

Local average treatment effect (LATE) The impact estimate produced by a regression discontinuity design. Valid only for units close to the eligibility cut-off, not for the full population of participants.
Lottery An RCT design that randomly selects who receives a programme, by public or private draw, among firms that already qualify. Works best when eligibility is clear and the programme is oversubscribed.



M

Managing Authority The national or regional body responsible for managing an ERDF or ESF+ programme, including reporting to the European Commission and, where an impact evaluation is planned, integrating randomisation into the programme’s design from the outset.
Matching A quasi-experimental method that pairs participants with non-participants who share similar observable characteristics, to mimic an RCT. Assumes there are no unobserved differences between matched firms that also affect the outcome.
Medium-term outcomes In a Theory of Change, the broader changes that accumulate from short-term outcomes, such as gains in firm-level productivity, tracked through Common Result Indicators (CRIs). Impact evaluation aims to show that a programme actually caused these changes, not just that they occurred.
Monitoring and evaluation (M&E) The ongoing collection of data on inputs, outputs, outcomes and participants to support day-to-day management and descriptive before-and-after comparisons. Unlike impact evaluation, M&E describes what is happening but cannot show that it happened because of the intervention.
Multiple treatment arms Randomly assigning different versions of a programme, with or without a control group, to learn which design works best rather than only whether the programme works at all.



O

Oslo Manual The OECD/Eurostat standard that defines innovation for statistical purposes, including the product innovation and process innovation definitions used on this site.
Outputs In a Theory of Change, the direct, countable results of a programme’s activities, such as the number of firms supported or grants awarded. What a programme produces, tracked through Common Output Indicators (COIs).



P

Power calculation A calculation, made before a programme launches, that combines the expected effect size, the variation between firms, the desired confidence level and the desired statistical power into the minimum sample size an evaluation needs.
Pre-post (before-after) design A quasi-experimental method that compares participants before and after a programme. It assumes nothing else affected outcomes over the same period, an assumption that rarely holds in practice.
Primary data Information collected directly from firms, individuals or organisations, through surveys or interviews conducted specifically for an evaluation. Gives more control over what is measured than secondary data, but costs more and takes longer to collect.
Process innovation A new or improved business process for one or more business functions that differs significantly from the firm’s previous business processes and has been implemented within the firm.
Product innovation A new or improved good or service that differs significantly from the firm’s previous goods or services and has been implemented on the market. Includes significant changes to the design of a good and digital goods or services; excludes the simple re-sale of new goods and changes of a solely aesthetic nature.



Q

Quasi-experimental methods Methods used to construct a comparison group after a programme has already launched, when randomisation was not built in from the start. They rely on assumptions, some of which cannot be tested, so the credibility of the evaluation depends on the credibility of those assumptions.



R

Random assignment A key element of beneficiary selection when RCTs are implemented, creating comparable groups at the programme’s onset. It differs from random selection in surveys.
Randomised controlled trial (RCT) An impact evaluation design that randomly assigns eligible participants to a treatment group, which receives the programme, and a control group, which does not. Because randomisation makes the two groups alike on average, the control group’s outcome shows what would have happened without the programme, without needing further assumptions about outcome trends.
Randomised intensities Randomly varying how much of a programme each participant receives, for example 100%, 50% or 0% of eligible employees, to study spillovers within or between firms.
Randomised phase-in A design in which everyone eventually receives a programme, in a randomly assigned order; firms still waiting act as the comparison group. Best when budget or capacity cannot cover everyone at once, though it limits how long the comparison can be observed.
Regression discontinuity design (RDD) A quasi-experimental method that compares participants just above an eligibility cut-off with those just below it. Because unobservable characteristics are unlikely to differ sharply at the cut-off, it needs weaker assumptions than other quasi-experimental methods, but it only estimates impact for firms near the cut-off, a local average treatment effect.
Research and Development (R&D) Creative and systematic work undertaken to increase the stock of knowledge, including knowledge of humankind, culture and society, and to devise new applications of available knowledge.



S

Secondary data Information that already exists in administrative records, such as business registries, tax data or a programme’s own management information system. Cheaper and covers larger samples than primary data, but may not include the specific outcomes an evaluation needs.
Selection bias Occurs when treatment (programme) assignment is not random, likely creating systematic differences between treatment and comparison groups. For example, firms with higher innovation levels may self-select into a programme offering innovation vouchers, so observed differences may stem from pre-existing characteristics rather than the intervention itself. RCTs mitigate this by randomising participants, so any outcome differences are due to the intervention only.
Short-term outcomes In a Theory of Change, the immediate changes that follow directly from a programme’s outputs, typically within one to two years, such as a firm adopting a new technology or a researcher filing a patent application.
Simple difference A quasi-experimental method that compares participants with non-participants. It assumes the only difference between the two groups is programme participation, which is often untrue since firms that choose to participate may differ systematically from those that do not.
SMART indicators Five characteristics of a well-defined evaluation indicator: Specific, Measurable, Attributable, Realistic and Targeted. Not to be confused with SMART Romania, the running example programme used elsewhere on this site.
Smart Specialisation Strategy A regional or national strategy that sets innovation priorities based on a region’s specific strengths, used to guide where Cohesion Policy innovation funding is targeted.
Spillover effects Indirect exposure of the comparison group to a programme’s benefits, for example when know-how spreads by word of mouth to non-participating firms. Related to contamination: it understates a programme’s measured impact by improving outcomes for firms that were not meant to receive support.
Statistical power The likelihood that an evaluation will detect a real programme effect if one actually exists. Higher power requires a larger sample, especially when the expected effect is small or firms vary widely.



T

Theory of Change (ToC) A structured account of how a policy’s activities are expected to lead, step by step, to its intended results, including the assumptions that must hold at each step. It builds on a programme’s intervention logic and shows what to measure and where the causal chain is most likely to break.
Treatment Group The group receiving the intervention or participating in the programme.



W

World Bank Enterprise Surveys A World Bank survey programme covering firm-level performance and business conditions. Another validated source of internationally comparable indicators for evaluation design.

title: Topic: intellectual property
text:
Patent applications and grants

Definition: Whether the firm filed for or obtained patents as a result of its innovation activities
Metric: Number of patent applications; number of patents granted; binary indicator
Data source: Administrative (EPO PATSTAT, national patent offices) or primary survey


Trademark and design registration

Definition: Whether the firm registered trademarks or designs to protect its market position
Metric: Number of trademarks or registered designs; binary indicator
Data source: Administrative (EUIPO records) or primary survey


Technology licensing

Definition: Whether the firm licenses technology to or from other companies – a measure of knowledge commercialisation
Metric: Binary indicator (licensor / licensee); value of licensing agreements (€)
Data source: Primary survey

title: Topic: digitalisation
text:
Digital technology adoption

Definition: Whether and which digital technologies the firm uses (cloud, AI, IoT, big data, etc.)
Metric: Number of digital technologies in use; binary indicators per technology type
Data source: Primary survey


Online sales share

Definition: Share of total sales conducted through digital channels
Metric: % of total turnover from online sales
Data source: Primary survey or administrative (VAT e-commerce records)


Digital investment

Definition: Spending on digital technologies and software
Metric: Total digital investment in €; % change from baseline
Data source: Primary survey or administrative


Digital skills of the workforce

Definition: Improvement in the digital capabilities of the firm’s employees
Metric: Share of employees with intermediate or advanced digital skills (%); binary indicator for digital training provision
Data source: Primary survey


Digital maturity score

Definition: Overall level of digitalisation across the firm’s strategy, processes, skills, and security
Metric: Composite index score based on standardised questions; % change from baseline
Data source: Primary survey

title: Topic: Research & Development activity
text:
Research & Development (R&D) engagement

Definition: Whether the firm conducts research and experimental development activities
Metric: Binary indicator (yes/no); frequency (continuous / occasional)
Data source: Primary survey or administrative (R&D tax credit records)


R&D expenditure

Definition: Total spending on in-house and contracted-out R&D activities
Metric: Total R&D expenditure in €; share of turnover spent on R&D (%)
Data source: Primary survey or administrative (R&D tax credit records, national R&D surveys)


R&D employment

Definition: Number of staff engaged in R&D activities
Metric: Full-time equivalent (FTE) R&D staff; share of total employees in R&D roles (%)
Data source: Primary survey or administrative


R&D additionality

Definition: Whether public support leads to an increase in total R&D spending (input additionality) or new products and processes (output additionality), rather than substituting for private investment
Metric: Difference in R&D expenditure or innovation output between treatment and control groups at endline, controlling for baseline
Data source: Primary survey or administrative; requires treatment/control comparison


Patent applications

Definition: Whether the firm has applied for or obtained patents as a result of its R&D activities
Metric: Number of patent applications filed; number of patents granted; binary indicator
Data source: Administrative (EPO PATSTAT, national patent office records) or primary survey

title: Topic: firm performance and growth
text:
Turnover growth

Definition: Change in total annual sales revenue over the evaluation period
Metric: % change in turnover from baseline to endline; log of turnover
Data source: Administrative (tax records, business registry) or primary survey


Value added

Definition: Value of output minus the value of intermediate inputs; a measure of the firm’s contribution to GDP
Metric: Total value added in € (turnover minus purchases of goods and services); % change over evaluation period
Data source: Administrative (tax records) or primary survey


Labour productivity

Definition: Output produced per unit of labour input – a core competitiveness indicator
Metric: Value added per employee (€); % change over evaluation period
Data source: Administrative or primary survey (requires both value added and employment data)


Total factor productivity (TFP)

Definition: Output not explained by inputs – captures how efficiently a firm uses all its resources
Metric: Estimated using production function methods (e.g. Olley-Pakes, Levinsohn-Petrin); requires data on output, capital, labour, and materials
Data source: Administrative (requires linked firm-level panel data)


Employment growth

Definition: Change in the number of people employed by the firm
Metric: % change in full-time equivalent (FTE) employees from baseline to endline; log of employment
Data source: Administrative (social security records, business registry) or primary survey


Wage growth

Definition: Change in average wages paid by the firm, reflecting improvements in job quality and productivity
Metric: % change in average gross wage per employee; total wage bill growth
Data source: Administrative (social security or tax records)


Export performance

Definition: Whether and how much the firm sells in foreign markets
Metric: Export participation (yes/no); share of turnover from exports (%); log of export value
Data source: Administrative (customs data) or primary survey


Firm survival

Definition: Whether the firm remains in operation over the evaluation period
Metric: Binary indicator (firm active / closed); survival rate across the sample
Data source: Administrative (business registry)

A note on energy data for Managing Authorities: Self-reported energy consumption data should be validated against energy bills wherever possible. The EENergy Programme requires firms to upload actual energy bills as supporting documentation – this approach is strongly recommended for any evaluation where energy consumption is a primary outcome. Smart meter data, where accessible, provides a more objective and continuous measure of energy use and eliminates recall bias. Data sharing agreements with energy providers may be needed to access this data and should be put in place at the program design stage.

title: Examples
text:
Spain: financial support to innovate


The problem
Market failures keep research and development (R&D) investment in Extremadura below its optimal level. Small and medium firms in the region under-invest in innovation, particularly in agriculture and the ecological transition.


What was done
The Regional Government of Extremadura (JUNTA) and the Extremadura Science and Technology Park Foundation (FUNDECYT-PCTEx) created an EU-funded matching grant programme for small and medium firms.
Each cycle awards €3.5 million in grants, up to €250,000 per firm (€138,000 on average), financing 35% to 80% of a firm’s proposed R&D investment.



What experimentation sought to answer

“What is the impact of R&D grants on SMEs’ business performance?”

Policy question›Eligibility›Lottery›Program›Follow-up›Impact

  The programmeMatching grants of up to EUR 250,000 per firm (average EUR 138,000) for R&D projects
  WhereExtremadura, Spain; regional government (JUNTA) with FUNDECYT-PCTEx, EU-funded
  Who is randomizedFirms: SME applicants, mainly agriculture and ecological transition, scored on 11 criteria
  The designBin-ranking RCT: the middle bin randomized, 22 funded vs. 34 not funded
  Outcomes trackedPrivate R&D investment, implementation success, expected sales growth
  Starting pointMarket failures keep regional R&D investment below its optimal level



From application to evidence

  Applications
  External scoring
  Middle-bin lottery
  R&D grants
  Follow-up survey



How the programme was tested
Extremadura ran an advertising campaign to attract at least 100 applicants. External reviewers scored every application on 11 objective criteria and grouped proposals into low, medium and high quality.


  Quality score

  
  High quality
  accepted and funded automatically

  
  Medium quality: 56 firms
  equally eligible, randomized by lottery
  22 funded · 34 not funded
  this band is the sample for study

  
  Low quality
  rejected automatically

  
  
  Only the middle band is randomized
  The strongest and weakest applicants
  are handled by the score, not the draw

  This design works well when eligibility criteria are clear and resources are limited.

Extremadura's bin-ranking design: only medium-quality applicants, the band where expected returns are least certain, are randomized.


Why this design. Strength: it leverages investment-return uncertainty for applications with unclear returns. Limitation: it requires a large sample size in the middle range (bin).


Randomisation successfully balanced key firm characteristics: the comparison group and the treatment group looked the same on average. There was no evidence of firms with certain characteristics dropping out of the study more than others (selective attrition) in follow-up survey responses.



What the programme achieved
Three months after receiving the grant, firms in the treatment group reported higher planned R&D investment and stronger confidence in their projects than the comparison group.


+48%
More planned R&D investment for 2025
€65,000 above the comparison-group average.


67%
Probability of successful implementation
Up from 16% without funding, according to expert priors.


×2
Expected sales growth, conditional on success
From 8% to 16% after receiving the grant, according to expert priors.



Over half of the comparison-group firms planned to continue their R&D projects using other funding or their own resources. Public R&D subsidies can significantly boost private investment, but careful targeting is needed to avoid simply displacing money firms would have spent anyway.

Czechia: light-touch support for SMEs


The problem
Entrepreneurial activity remains low in Czech regions hit by the decline of the coal industry. These regions need to diversify away from carbon-intensive industries and grow their private sector.
In September 2022, the European Commission approved the Just Transition Programme (JTP): €1.641 billion for business R&D, post-mining regeneration, skills, clean energy and the circular economy in the Moravian-Silesian, Ústí and Karlovy Vary regions.
A key part of the JTP is a voucher scheme for entrepreneurs: up to €21,100 for business development, up to €42,200 for innovation, and up to €21,100 for digital transformation.


What was done
The World Bank tested two light-touch, complementary pilots that add skills support on top of the voucher scheme.
Smart Start (Moravian-Silesian region): seven workshops teaching a scientific approach to decision-making under uncertainty, covering risk versus uncertainty, hypothesis testing and A/B testing, aimed at voucher recipients and other interested firms.
AI Klub (Ústí and Karlovy Vary regions): five hands-on workshops on using AI for efficiency, marketing, sales, product development and financial management, with peer-to-peer exchange between firms.

Croatia: matching businesses with scientists


The problem
Firms and scientists in Croatia struggle to collaborate: information frictions, uncertain transaction costs and limited outreach budgets get in the way, especially for small and medium firms.
Only 8% of Croatian firms collaborate with higher education institutions, far below the EU average. A World Bank survey found that 47% of firms lacked information about relevant scientists.


What was done
The World Bank, the Innovation Centre Nikola Tesla and the Ministry of Science, Education and Youth designed “Scinergy”, a business-science matchmaking pilot targeting fields such as AI, energy and biotechnology.
Matched firms and scientists took part in a two-day matchmaking event in February 2024: “speed-dating” sessions followed by joint workshops, plus legal and communication support to help pairs plan R&D projects together.



What experimentation sought to answer

title: Examples
section: Europe: grants for SME energy efficiency
text:
Europe: grants for SME energy efficiency


The problem
Energy efficiency is one of the cheapest ways for a firm to cut energy use and costs, yet most European SMEs invest little in it. Among the firms that applied to this programme, only 22% had invested in energy efficiency in the year before applying, even though 62% already monitored their energy use and almost all planned some form of capital investment. Advice on its own was not turning plans into purchases.


What was done
The European Commission (DG GROW and EISMEA), the Enterprise Europe Network (EEN) and the World Bank ran the EENergy pilot, funded by the EU Single Market Programme.
On top of the advisory support EEN advisors already provide, the pilot offered a reimbursement grant of up to EUR 10,000 for energy-efficiency measures: equipment and installations, consultancy, or staff training. The evaluation was designed into the programme from the start, before the first call opened.



What experimentation sought to answer

“Does money on top of advice change what small firms invest in, and does it cut their energy use?”

Policy question›Eligibility›Lottery›Program›Follow-up›Impact


The programme

  The programmeEENergy: a reimbursement grant of up to EUR 10,000 for equipment, consultancy or training, on top of standard EEN advisory services
  Where34 European countries; European Commission (DG GROW, EISMEA) and Enterprise Europe Network with the World Bank, funded by the EU Single Market Programme
  Who is randomized1,964 eligible SMEs across two open calls: 54% micro, 36% small, 9% medium-sized; 36% in manufacturing
  The designSimple lottery among eligible applicants, run separately for each call and stratified by consortium and advisor: 986 offered the grant vs. 978 receiving advisory services only
  Outcomes trackedEnergy-efficiency and renewable investment, energy use and spending, energy management practices, revenue, profits and employment
  Starting pointOnly 22% of applicant firms had invested in energy efficiency in the year before the programme, although 62% already monitored their energy use



From application to evidence

  Two open calls
  Eligibility check
  Lottery
  Grants & advisory services
  Follow-up surveys



How the programme was tested
Firms applied in two open calls, from February to May 2024 and from December 2024 to February 2025. Applications were screened against the EU definition of an SME and against programme requirements, including an energy-efficiency action plan agreed with an EEN advisor and a target of at least 5% lower energy consumption. Eligible firms then entered a lottery, run separately for each call and stratified by consortium and advisor characteristics, so that funded and unfunded firms came from the same pool and worked with comparable advisors.


  
  3,000+
  applications

  

  
  1,964
  eligible firms

  

  
  LOTTERY
  every firm, the same chance

  
  

  
  986 offered a grant
  up to EUR 10,000, plus advice

  
  978 standard group
  advisory services only

Every firm in the study had already cleared eligibility and was working with an EEN advisor, so the lottery isolates the effect of the money rather than the advice.


Why this design. Strength: because the grant was drawn by lottery among firms that all received the same advisory service, the comparison separates the effect of the cash from the effect of the advice, across 34 countries at once. Limitation: firms offered the grant answered follow-up surveys far more often than the standard group (91% against 65%), so the estimates depend on statistical corrections for who responded.



What the programme achieved
One year on, the grant had changed what firms bought and how they managed energy. Total energy-related investment was about EUR 9,700 higher per firm in the grant group, almost all of it capital spending, with renewable-energy installations the single largest category.


+26 pp
Firms investing in energy efficiency
43% of firms offered the grant made an energy-efficiency investment, against 17% of the standard group.


×3
Firms investing in renewables
The share investing in renewable energy rose from 10% to about 30%.


+31 pp
Firms setting energy-reduction goals
83% of the grant group set energy-reduction goals, against 52% of the standard group, alongside more regular energy monitoring.


The response was strongest among the smallest firms. Renewable-energy investment rose by 22 percentage points among micro and small firms, against 5 points among medium-sized firms. The fixed EUR 10,000 was worth roughly 5% of annual revenue for the median micro firm, but only 0.1% for the median medium-sized firm, which is the clearest explanation on offer for the gap.

Averaged across all firms, no reduction in electricity consumption or total energy spending was detectable one year after the grants, and there was no detectable effect on revenue, profits or employment. Savings did appear for particular groups: electricity consumption fell by about 10% among micro and small firms, and electricity spending by about 20% among firms in the second call. The practical lesson for programme design is to scale a fixed grant to firm size, or to target smaller firms, and to justify it on investment and management change rather than on short-run business performance.


To confirm before publishing. Two points need a final check against the report: the exact number of submitted applications across both calls (the report gives 1,585 and 1,639 in the text, but 1,469 and 1,639 in the applications figure), and whether a public link to the final report and the 2-pager can be added here alongside the trial registration (AEA RCT Registry, AEARCTR-0015124).

title: Examples
section: Bulgaria: human-led versus AI-led business consulting
text:
Bulgaria: human-led versus AI-led business consulting


The problem
Northern Bulgaria’s micro and small enterprises (MSEs) – over 98% of firms in the region – lag far behind Southern Bulgaria and the EU average. Depopulation and aging have left “ghost towns” with shrinking labor pools and declining customer bases, and managerial skills, often picked up informally, limit the uptake of modern business practices. AI adoption is strikingly low: just 6.5% of firms in the region use AI, against an EU average of 13.5%.


What is being tested
The Bulgarian Small and Medium Enterprises Promotion Agency (BSMEPA) is launching a programme that pairs group training in managerial skills with one of three ways of delivering further support: one-on-one human-led consulting, a subscription to an off-the-shelf AI platform such as ChatGPT Premium, or a customised AI tool that proactively nudges managers toward it. The aim is to find out whether AI-led alternatives can match costly human consulting at a fraction of the price.



What the evaluation aims to answer

“Can lower-cost, AI-led consulting match the effectiveness of traditional human-led consulting for small firms?”

Policy question›Eligibility›Lottery›Program›Follow-up›Impact


The programme

  The programmeGroup training in managerial skills, then one of three support modes: human-led consulting, an AI subscription, or a customised AI-led consulting tool
  WhereNorthern Bulgaria; Bulgarian Small and Medium Enterprises Promotion Agency (BSMEPA)
  Who is randomized600 MSEs (fewer than 50 employees) in retail, agricultural processing, services and manufacturing, stratified by sector, region and owner gender
  The designFour-arm RCT: pure control, training + human consulting, training + AI subscription, training + AI-led consulting tool (150 firms per arm)
  Outcomes trackedFirm sales, sales per worker, profits and exports; management practices, foreign-market knowledge, access to suppliers, finance and customers
  Starting pointMSEs report 88% lower sales per worker than larger firms on average, and only 6.5% of regional firms use AI, against an EU average of 13.5%



From application to evidence

  Recruitment & applications
  Random assignment
  Training & consulting rollout
  Endline survey
  Follow-up survey



How the programme is designed
The Agency will mobilise applicants directly across northern Bulgaria; up to 450 eligible firms will be offered business support, with no applicant guaranteed a place. Once 600 eligible firms have applied, firms are randomly allocated, stratified by sector, region and owner gender, to a pure control group or one of three treatment arms.


  
  600
  eligible MSEs

  
  
  
  
  

  
  150 control
  no training or consulting

  
  150 training + human-led consulting
  one-on-one, in person

  
  150 training + AI subscription
  e.g. ChatGPT Premium

  
  150 training + AI-led consulting tool
  proactive nudges

600 eligible MSEs are randomly assigned in equal shares to a control group and three treatment arms, so each AI-based alternative can be compared directly to human-led consulting.


Why this design. Strength: putting human-led consulting and two AI-based alternatives in the same trial, against the same control group, lets the evaluation rank all three by cost-effectiveness rather than comparing each in isolation. Limitation: with 150 firms per arm, the study is powered to detect a change in sales of around 26% or more, so more modest effects could go undetected.



What the evaluation will tell us


Human-led vs AI-led
Whether a customised, proactively-nudging AI tool can approach the effectiveness of costly one-on-one human consulting, at a much lower marginal cost.


Off-the-shelf vs custom AI
Whether simply subscribing managers to an existing tool like ChatGPT Premium is enough, or whether a tailored, proactive AI platform is needed to change business practices.


How durable are the gains
Whether improvements from AI-enabled consulting persist for longer than from human-led consulting, since managers keep the ability to self-serve after the programme ends.



The main risks to the evaluation are insufficient take-up of consulting or AI services, and non-random attrition between the baseline and the two follow-up rounds. The team is mitigating these with in-person mobilisation to build the applicant pool, and by collecting detailed contact and backup information from every participant to support tracking through fall 2027.

title: Examples
section: Poland: AI assistance for smarter Horizon Europe applications
text:
Poland: AI assistance for smarter Horizon Europe applications


The problem
Polish SMEs underperform in Horizon Europe, the EU’s flagship innovation funding programme: a 16.5% success rate, against an EU-27 average of 20.3%. Funding is also highly concentrated – just 11 SMEs account for roughly a third of all Polish projects. A previous support scheme, “Grants for Eurogrants,” converted only 400 of about 1,700 applications into signed contracts, and just 19 firms ultimately secured EU funding. Only 20.1% of firms report knowing PARP, the agency responsible for this support.


What is being tested
The Polish Agency for Enterprise Development (PARP) is testing a three-stage pilot: behavioural messaging to raise awareness of its support; a machine-learning model that scores firms’ likelihood of Horizon Europe success, used to target encouragement calls; and an AI-based advisory tool paired with a human “technology scout” for firms that express interest in applying.



What the evaluation aims to answer

“Can behavioural messaging, algorithmic targeting and AI-assisted advice raise the number and quality of Polish Horizon Europe applications?”

Policy question›Eligibility›Lottery›Program›Follow-up›Impact


The programme

  The programmeA three-stage pilot: behavioural outreach messaging, machine-learning targeting with encouragement calls, and AI-tool-plus-technology-scout application support
  WherePoland; Polish Agency for Enterprise Development (PARP)
  Who is randomized~120,000 SMEs reached with outreach messages; ~11,000 Horizon-eligible firms in the targeting stage; up to ~500 interested firms in the support stage
  The designThree nested RCTs: a messaging A/B/C test, ranked-vs-random encouragement calls, and AI-tool-and-scout support (~200 firms) vs. a waitlist
  Outcomes trackedEmail/ad engagement, applications to PARP and Horizon Europe, blind-rated application quality, funding success, and firm employment, revenue and survival
  Starting pointJust 16.5% of Polish Horizon Europe applications succeed, against an EU-27 average of 20.3%, and only 20.1% of firms report knowing PARP



From application to evidence

  Outreach messaging
  ML targeting
  Encouragement calls
  Support sign-up
  AI-tool & scout support



How the programme is designed
Three experiments are nested inside PARP’s own application funnel. First, roughly 120,000 SMEs are randomly shown one of three outreach messages, from a plain fact-based announcement to versions adding behavioural nudges and information about the new AI-powered support. Second, from a pool of about 11,000 Horizon-eligible firms, one half is ranked by a machine-learning model trained on past Horizon winners; the top 500 ranked firms and 500 randomly-selected firms then both receive an encouragement call. Third, among the roughly 400–500 firms that register interest in extra support, 200 are randomly selected for immediate access to an AI advisory tool and a technology scout, while the remainder are waitlisted.


  
  Stage 1: Outreach
  ~120,000 SMEs
  3 randomised messages (A/B/C)

  
  Stage 2: Targeting
  ~11,000 eligible firms
  ranked (500 called) vs. not-ranked (500 called)

  
  Stage 3: Support
  ~400–500 interested firms
  ~200 AI tool + scout vs. waitlist

  
  

  Each stage is a separate randomisation, feeding firms forward into PARP's existing application funnel.

Three nested experiments track firms from broad outreach through algorithmic targeting to intensive AI-and-scout application support.


Why this design. Strength: nesting three experiments inside PARP’s own application funnel means each stage’s estimate is drawn from firms who arrive naturally through the programme, not an artificial sample. Limitation: because later stages depend on take-up from earlier ones, the sample shrinks at each step, leaving less statistical power for the innermost support experiment.



What the evaluation will tell us


Does messaging move firms?
Whether behavioural nudges – social proof, urgency framing, expected-value framing – raise click-throughs and registrations more than PARP’s standard, fact-based messaging.


Can an algorithm find promising firms?
Whether a machine-learning “Horizon potential score,” trained on past winners, identifies firms more likely to submit competitive applications than outreach targeted at random.


Does AI-assisted support raise quality?
Whether pairing an AI advisory tool with a human technology scout increases application rates, application quality and ultimately funding success, compared with PARP’s standard waitlist resources.



The clearest risk to implementation is legal: whether informing firms that a machine-learning model identified them as “high-potential” is compatible with EU data-protection law is still under review, and may limit how the targeting stage can be communicated. The team is also tracking whether firms treat encouragement phone calls as credible outreach from PARP rather than as spam.

title: Examples
section: Romania (North-East): AI assistance for smarter grant reviews
text:
Romania (North-East): AI assistance for smarter grant reviews


The problem
At Romania’s Regional Development Agencies, grant application reviews are slow and inconsistent. The 2023 Microenterprise call at the North-East RDA took roughly seven months from submission to contract, generated 50 technical-financial appeals and 19 contracting appeals, and disadvantaged smaller firms: enterprises under two years old, with no employees or turnover below 250,000 RON, succeeded only 14% of the time, against over 90% for firms with turnover of 1.5–2 million RON. Many applicants turn to a large consultancy industry – an estimated €527 million in annual turnover across 1,500 firms – just to navigate the process.


What is being tested
The North-East Regional Development Agency (RDA), with the automation company UiPath, has built an AI decision-support tool that benchmarks proposed budgets, flags risks, and supports reviewers on eligibility and quality criteria. It is being embedded in the 2026 Microenterprise Growth Grant Call (about €30 million), with reviewers randomly assigned to work with or without the tool, and funded projects randomly assigned to AI-assisted or standard monitoring.



What the evaluation aims to answer

“Can an AI decision-support tool make public grant reviews faster, more consistent and better targeted, without compromising fairness?”

Policy question›Eligibility›Lottery›Program›Follow-up›Impact


The programme

  The programmeAn AI decision-support tool, co-developed with UiPath, that benchmarks budgets, flags risks and supports eligibility and quality scoring for grant reviewers
  WhereNorth-East Romania; Regional Development Agency (RDA), embedded in the 2026 Microenterprise Growth Grant Call (≈€30 million)
  Who is randomized~1,000 expressions of interest and ~800 full proposals, reviewed by 30–40 trained reviewers; ~150 funded projects
  The designMulti-phase RCT: reviewers randomised to AI-assisted or human-only review at each stage; ~150 grants allocated by lottery within score bands; funded projects randomised to AI-assisted or standard monitoring
  Outcomes trackedReview time and scores, clarification requests and appeals, on-time disbursement, and funded-firm survival, employment, revenue and investment
  Starting pointThe 2023 call took roughly seven months from submission to contract; firms under two years old or with no employees had a 14% success rate, against over 90% for the highest-turnover firms



From application to evidence

  Expression of interest
  AI-assisted or human review
  Full proposal & review
  Funding lottery
  AI-assisted or standard monitoring



How the programme is designed
Around 1,000 expressions of interest are expected, each assigned to one of 30–40 trained reviewers who are randomly given, or not given, access to the AI tool; reviewers cycle between AI-assisted and unassisted batches so the comparison is not confounded by reviewer ability. Roughly 800 full proposals then go through the same randomised review process. Of the approximately 600 proposals that clear eligibility checks, about 150 are funded through a lottery run separately within AI-assisted and human-only score bands, so funding decisions stay comparable across review modes. Funded projects are then randomly assigned to AI-assisted or standard monitoring during implementation.


  
  1,000
  expressions of interest

  

  
  800
  full proposals

  

  
  600 eligible
  funding lottery, by score band

  
  
  

  
  75 funded: AI monitoring
  automated risk flags

  
  75 funded: standard monitoring
  human oversight only

Reviewers are randomly assigned to work with or without the AI tool at each review stage (not shown); funded projects are then randomly split between AI-assisted and standard monitoring.


Why this design. Strength: randomising AI access at the reviewer-proposal level, with each reviewer cycling between AI-assisted and unassisted batches, isolates the effect of the tool from differences between reviewers. Limitation: because a reviewer with AI access can choose how much to rely on it, the design measures the effect of being offered AI support (intention-to-treat), not of using it, though usage telemetry will help distinguish the two.



What the evaluation will tell us


Faster, more consistent reviews
Whether AI-assisted reviewers complete assessments faster, and with fewer clarification requests or appeals, than reviewers working without AI support.


Sharper targeting of promising firms
Whether the relationship between evaluation scores and firms’ later performance is stronger when those scores were produced with AI assistance.


Fair treatment across firm types
Whether AI assistance changes the pattern of scores and funding by owner gender, firm age and sector, as part of a pre-registered bias audit.



The central safeguard against biased AI outputs is a systematic audit of scoring patterns across firm groups after the expression-of-interest phase; if the audit finds significant disparities, the underlying prompts and models will be reviewed and adjusted before the full-proposal stage goes ahead.

title: Examples
section: Romania (South Muntenia): the returns to innovation subsidies
text:
Romania (South Muntenia): the returns to innovation subsidies


The problem
South Muntenia is a lagging EU region, ranked 243rd of EU regions on the Regional Innovation Scoreboard, with an Innovation Readiness Index of just 28. Only 6.3% of firms are classified as innovative, and just 1.4% of the workforce works in high-tech sectors. Between 2014 and 2020, Romania allocated €1.6 billion to public research institutes but only €74 million to private firms, and the region hosts just 3% of the country’s research infrastructure.


What is being tested
The South Muntenia Regional Development Agency (SM-RDA) is allocating €24.8 million in innovation subsidies to SMEs, cross-randomised with a management-training programme on change and innovation culture. Grants are assigned through a two-stage design: geographic or sector clusters are randomly assigned different shares of funded firms, and firms within each cluster are then randomly selected to receive funding – allowing the evaluation to separate a firm’s own private return from spillovers onto its neighbours.



What the evaluation aims to answer

“Do the private returns to innovation subsidies for SMEs exceed their social returns, once spillovers to other firms are taken into account?”

Policy question›Eligibility›Lottery›Program›Follow-up›Impact


The programme

  The programmeInnovation subsidy grants (50–70% co-financed by firms) for R&D projects, cross-randomised with a management-training programme on change and innovation culture
  WhereSouth Muntenia, Romania; South Muntenia Regional Development Agency (SM-RDA), €24.8 million SME innovation grant allocation
  Who is randomized≈900 SMEs across 100 geographic or sectoral clusters (≈9 firms per cluster), excluding agricultural firms
  The designTwo-stage RCT: clusters randomised to 0%, 33%, 66% or 100% funding intensity, then firms randomised to funding within each cluster; management training cross-randomised at firm level
  Outcomes trackedShort-run revenue, inputs, profit, productivity, investment, pricing and product variety; medium- to long-run technology adoption, new products, licensing and patenting
  Starting pointOnly 6.3% of firms in the region are classified as innovative and just 1.4% of the workforce works in high-tech sectors, with an Innovation Readiness Index of 28



From application to evidence

  Call for proposals
  Cluster formation
  Cluster-level intensity
  Firm-level lottery
  Grant & monitoring



How the programme is designed
After the call for proposals closes, applicant firms are grouped into roughly 100 clusters based on geographic or sectoral proximity. Each cluster is then randomly assigned a funding intensity – the share of its firms that will receive a subsidy, set at 0%, 33%, 66% or 100% – and firms within the cluster are randomly selected for funding up to that share. Comparing outcomes across clusters with different intensities isolates spillover effects, while comparing funded and unfunded firms within the same cluster isolates each firm’s own private return.


  Cluster-level intensity (randomised across ≈100 clusters)

  
  0% funded

  
  33% funded

  
  66% funded

  
  100% funded

  
  Example cluster at 33% intensity: 9 firms, 3 randomly funded

  
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
  
  funded
  funded
  funded

  Comparing across clusters isolates spillovers; comparing within a cluster isolates each firm's own private return.

Clusters are randomly assigned a funding intensity; within each cluster, firms are then randomly selected for funding up to that share.


Why this design. Strength: varying funding intensity across clusters, on top of randomising which firms within a cluster are funded, lets the evaluation separate a firm’s private return from spillovers onto its neighbours and competitors. Limitation: the design captures spillovers within a cluster but not across cluster boundaries, which the team plans to approximate separately with a structural, network-based model.



What the evaluation will tell us


Do subsidies pay off for the firm?
Whether receiving an innovation subsidy raises a firm’s revenue, profits, productivity and investment in the short run, and its technology adoption and patenting over the longer run.


Do the gains spread, or just shift?
Whether firms in higher-intensity clusters see larger productivity gains through knowledge diffusion, or whether funded firms instead grow at competitors’ expense.


Does training make subsidies work harder?
Whether pairing the grant with training on change management and innovation culture strengthens firms’ ability to absorb and use the funding.



The main risk to the spillover analysis is statistical power: if spillovers turn out to be smaller than about 8 percentage points (roughly a third of the expected direct subsidy effect), that part of the analysis will be underpowered. Even so, the team notes the resulting estimates will still provide useful benchmarks for calibrating models of innovation diffusion, an area where experimental evidence remains scarce.

title: Examples
section: Earlier work by the EuroCOMP Lab team: Digitrans
text:
Earlier work by the EuroCOMP Lab team: Digitrans


The problem
Small businesses in Bulgaria, Poland and Slovakia show limited adoption of digital tools beyond what regulation or the financial sector requires. The 2022 Digital Economy and Society Index places all three countries in the bottom quartile of EU members for business digitalisation.
Current public support programmes in the region largely overlook this: MSMEs account for 98% of businesses and two-thirds of employment, yet most programmes still emphasise technology adoption and financial assistance, leaving the managerial and organisational capabilities firms need to make use of new tools unaddressed.


What was done
The World Bank designed Digitrans, a standardised support instrument tested across Bulgaria, Poland and Slovakia, integrating a financial subsidy with technical assistance to address both resource and capability constraints.
The financial subsidy provides up to €2,000 per firm towards the cost of adopting digital business tools. The technical assistance component adds a 10-week programme of diagnostic assessment, group training and one-to-one advisory support.



What experimentation sought to answer

“Does pairing technical assistance with a financial subsidy improve MSME digitalisation outcomes more than a subsidy alone?”

Policy question›Eligibility›Lottery›Program›Follow-up›Impact


The programme

  The programmeA financial subsidy of up to EUR 2,000 per firm, with a subset of firms also receiving a 10-week technical assistance programme
  WhereBulgaria, Poland and Slovakia; World Bank Digitrans pilot, EU-funded
  Who is randomized629 MSMEs with 5–35 employees and at least 12 months trading, drawn from over 1,600 applications
  The designThree-arm RCT, stratified by country, firm size and digital sophistication: comparison (209), subsidy only (210), subsidy plus technical assistance (210)
  Outcomes trackedDigital tool adoption and usage, managerial and organisational change, firm performance
  Starting pointSmall businesses show limited digital adoption beyond what regulation or banks require



From application to evidence

  Applications
  Eligibility & interview
  Random assignment
  Subsidy & support
  Follow-up survey



How the programme was tested
Firms applied through an open call across Bulgaria, Poland and Slovakia in 2024, and those meeting the eligibility criteria completed a baseline interview. Eligible firms were then randomly assigned by the World Bank into one of three groups, with randomisation stratified within each country by firm size and digital sophistication so that groups were balanced from the outset.


  
  629
  randomised firms

  

  
  STRATIFIED LOTTERY
  by country, size and digital sophistication

  
  
  
  

  
  209 comparison group
  benchmarking report only

  
  210 financial subsidy
  subsidy plus benchmarking report

  
  210 subsidy + technical assistance
  the full support package

Randomisation was stratified within each country by firm size and digital sophistication, splitting 629 eligible firms into a comparison group and two support groups of about 210 firms each.


Why this design. Strength: a three-arm design separates the effect of money from the effect of capability-building support, rather than only comparing supported firms to unsupported ones. Limitation: it needs a larger sample than a simple two-arm trial to detect the same effect size, since firms are split three ways.


Allocation resulted in balanced groups across a broad range of firm characteristics, creating a solid foundation for rigorous impact evaluation. There was no evidence of systematic differences between groups at baseline, so later changes can be reliably attributed to the support received rather than to pre-existing differences.



What the programme achieved


2.5x
Digital tool usage is 2.5x higher with combined support
Firms that received both types of support increased their digital tool usage intensity more than twice as much as those with a subsidy alone.


2x
Managerial changes are more common with technical assistance
Firms in the combined support group were twice as likely to introduce internal organisational and managerial changes.


82% vs 67%
Combined support leads to deeper use of digital tools
Firms with technical assistance made better use of advanced software functions: 82% used CRM systems for client communication, against 67% in the subsidy-only group.



Firms receiving only a financial subsidy typically limited their spending to the subsidy value, with no meaningful increase in the sophistication of tools available to them. Effective digitalisation support needs to go beyond subsidising technology purchases: the benefits of combined support were especially strong among smaller firms, firms with low initial digital capabilities, service-sector firms and women-led businesses.

title: Examples
text:
Examples from beyond the Lab

Colombia: Scaling up management consulting


The problem
Colombian auto parts manufacturers show wide variation in management practices, and weaker practices are closely tied to lower productivity. Structured, hands-on management consulting can improve how firms are run, but delivering it in a resource-intensive, one-on-one format is costly – a cost that can be prohibitive for small and medium firms to finance on their own, and for governments seeking to support large numbers of firms at once.


What was done
The World Bank, in partnership with the Government of Colombia, tested two lower-cost ways to deliver management consulting to small and medium manufacturers: individual, firm-by-firm consulting delivered by local teams, and a more novel group-based model that works with several firms together to bring costs down further.
Every participating firm, including the comparison group, first received a diagnostic assessment of its management practices across five areas – logistics, human resources, finance, marketing and sales, and production – carried out by a team of specialist consultants.




What experimentation sought to answer

“Can lower-cost individual or group-based consulting improve small and medium firms’ management practices and performance?”

Policy question›Eligibility›Lottery›Program›Follow-up›Impact


The programme

  The programmeA diagnostic for every firm, followed by individual or group-based management consulting
  WhereColombia — auto parts manufacturing sector
  Who is randomized159 eligible firms (manufacturers, tier 1/2 suppliers, 2+ years old, 10+ workers), in 53 matched triplets
  The designThree-arm RCT: comparison, individual consulting (~US$28,950/firm), group consulting (~US$10,500/firm)
  Outcomes trackedManagement practices; employment, sales, value-added and profits via administrative records
  Starting pointBaseline management scores ranged from 43 to 51 out of 100 across practice areas



From application to evidence

  Applications
  Diagnostic phase
  Matched-triplet lottery
  Consulting delivered
  Outcome tracking



How the programme was tested
218 firms applied to Colombia’s Programa de Extensionismo Tecnológico. After screening for eligibility – established auto parts manufacturers that were tier 1 or 2 suppliers, at least two years old, with at least ten employees, and located in Antioquia, Cundinamarca, Valle del Cauca or the Eje Cafetero – 159 firms formed the final sample.
Firms were then grouped into 53 matched triplets, formed to minimise differences in location, size, labor productivity and management practices between the three firms in each triplet. Within each triplet, firms were randomly allocated to a comparison group, individual consulting, or group consulting.


  
  159
  eligible firms

  

  
  53 MATCHED TRIPLETS
  by location, size, productivity, practices

  
  
  
  

  
  53 comparison group
  diagnostic only, no consulting

  
  53 individual consulting
  ~US$28,950/firm, over 6 months

  
  53 group consulting
  ~US$10,500/firm, in groups of 3–8

Firms were matched into triplets before randomisation, then randomly allocated within each triplet to a comparison group, individual consulting, or group consulting.


Why this design. Strength: matching firms into triplets before randomising keeps the three groups closely balanced on size, productivity and starting management practices, even with a modest overall sample. Limitation: with only 53 firms in each arm, the design has less statistical power to detect small effects than a larger, simple two-arm trial.



What the programme achieved


+9 pp
Management practices improved in both groups
Individual and group consulting each raised firms’ management practice scores by around 9 percentage points on average, relative to a baseline of 56%.


+28% to +33%
Sales and profits rose for group-consulting firms
Firms receiving group-based consulting saw significant gains in sales, value-added and profits; the individual programme’s effects on firm performance were smaller and not statistically significant.


US$273,000
Estimated average annual profit increase, group consulting
At a cost of about US$10,500 per firm, the estimated profit gains from group consulting paid back the programme’s cost within about a month.



Group-consulting firms reported far more contact with each other after the programme than before it: business links between study firms were almost non-existent at baseline, but around half of group participants said they still communicated with other group members roughly a year later, and firms whose management practices changed the most tended to be grouped with others who also improved the most – evidence that peer learning, not just lower delivery cost, contributed to the group programme’s stronger results on firm performance.


The group programme’s rollout was delayed by more than a year due to a budgetary payment delay, and only 68% of group-assigned firms completed the intervention, compared with 87% for the individually delivered programme. Delays like this are a practical risk to weigh when comparing the cost-effectiveness of different delivery models.


Further reading

<span class="fr-cite">Iacovone, L., Maloney, W. F., & McKenzie, D. (2022). Improving management with individual and group-based consulting: Results from a randomized experiment in Colombia. <em>Review of Economic Studies</em>, 89(1), 346–371.</span>
<a href="https://documents.worldbank.org/en/publication/documents-reports/documentdetail/198461559921937913">Read the paper →</a>




Yemen: Testing whether internships help youth find work


The problem
Young jobseekers in Yemen often face a catch-22: firms are reluctant to hire someone without prior work experience, yet that experience is hard to gain without first being hired. Early jobs matter because they build both job-specific and soft skills, but firms may under-invest in providing them – a reluctance that can be sharper still in a fragile, conflict-affected setting. Job opportunities for young graduates were also increasingly scarce following Yemen’s 2011–12 political crisis.


What was done
The Enterprise Revitalization and Employment Pilot (EREP) tested a subsidised-internship model: the program paid half the cost of a six-month internship, with the host firm covering the rest, and matched applicants to firms based on the firm’s stated requirements. Recent graduates in Sanaa and Aden applied online and were screened for eligibility before being considered.




What experimentation sought to answer

“Can a subsidised matchmaking program help young jobseekers gain their first work experience, and does that experience translate into better employment outcomes afterward?”

Policy question›Eligibility›Application›Random assignment›Matchmaking›Follow-up›Impact


The programme

  The programmeEnterprise Revitalization and Employment Pilot (EREP), internship component — matching grants covering half the cost of a six-month internship, plus matchmaking between graduates and firms
  WhereRepublic of Yemen — Sanaa and Aden
  Who is randomized583 eligible youth (Yemeni, Sanaa/Aden residents, graduated within 2 years), to treatment (430) or control (153)
  The designRCT; treatment group offered matchmaking to internships subsidised at 50% of cost, for up to six months
  Outcomes trackedEmployment, months worked and earnings, via a follow-up phone survey
  Starting point3,487 eligible youth applied; 500 were randomly invited to a two-day basic skills training (477 attended)



From application to evidence

  Applications
  Skills-training invitation
  Random assignment
  Matchmaking
  Follow-up survey



How the programme was tested
The program launched in August 2013 through a project website, media events and campus outreach. Applications ran from October to December 2013, closing with 3,487 eligible applicants. Of these, 500 were randomly invited to a two-day basic skills training – chosen with probability proportional to the demand for their specialisation – and 477 attended.
The resulting experimental sample of 583 individuals was randomly assigned, within strata defined by specialisation and city, to a treatment group of 430 (offered matchmaking to a subsidised internship) or a control group of 153. Eleven human resource advisors then matched treatment-group applicants to firms based on the firm’s requirements, sending CVs for firms to interview and decide whether to offer a placement.


  
  3,487
  eligible applicants

  

  
  500 invited to training
  477 attended

  

  
  583 experimental sample
  assigned within 39 strata

  
  
  

  
  430 treatment
  offered matchmaking

  
  153 control
  no internship match

Applicants were randomly invited to basic skills training, then the resulting sample was randomly assigned, within specialisation-and-city strata, to a treatment group offered internship matchmaking or a control group.


Why this design. Strength: randomising within strata defined by specialisation and city, among applicants who had already been invited to training, helps ensure the treatment and control groups started out comparable in skills and local job-market conditions. Limitation: more applicants were assigned to treatment than there were internship placements available, so actual take-up (36.7%) fell well below the treatment assignment rate – which is why the study reports both an intention-to-treat effect and a larger effect scaled up for those who actually took up an internship.



What the programme achieved


+17 pp / +42 pp
More likely to have worked at all in 2014
Being offered internship matchmaking raised the chance of having worked at all during 2014 by 17 percentage points on an intention-to-treat basis, and by 42 percentage points among those who actually took up an internship, relative to a 61% employment rate in the control group.


+0.35 s.d. / +0.85 s.d.
Employment gains persisted months after the internship ended
On a standardised index of employment outcomes measured three to five months after internships ended, effects remained statistically significant – 0.35 standard deviations on an intention-to-treat basis, and 0.85 standard deviations for those who took up an internship.


36.7%
Take-up among those assigned to treatment
Only 158 of the 430 people assigned to treatment were actually matched to and completed an internship placement, reflecting how binding capacity constraints were relative to demand for internship positions.



The internship raised employment more for male applicants than for female applicants, so the program did not close the pre-existing gender gap in employment outcomes. Because the evaluation covers only one year of the program rather than the two originally planned, the study had limited statistical power to say precisely how much smaller the effect was for women.


Conflict escalated partway through the program: Houthi forces took control of Sanaa in September 2014, and the second year of the pilot was cancelled, roughly halving the intended sample and reducing statistical power. The follow-up survey was also fielded earlier and more narrowly than planned, amid displacement and shortages of fuel, electricity and water. It also remains possible that some of the employment gains for treated youth came partly at the expense of other jobseekers in the economy – a general equilibrium effect this study could not measure.


Further reading

<span class="fr-cite">McKenzie, D., Assaf, N., & Cusolito, A. P. (2016). The demand for, and impact of, youth internships: Evidence from a randomized experiment in Yemen. <em>IZA Journal of Labor & Development</em>, 5(1), 1–15.</span>
