title: RCTs: why and when
section: When not to run an RCT
text:
When not to run an RCT


01

Not the right tool
The question is excellent but is not about impact, for example satisfaction with services or cost per service. Monitoring and feedback data are easier and do not need a counterfactual.



02

Not yet
The theory of change is not clear, or implementation is unlikely to work because the markets to serve do not exist.



03

Statistically not feasible
Too few units or too little money. Large indirect or spillover effects you cannot measure (Spillovers alone are not a reason to drop an RCT: if expected, they can be designed for and measured (see Step 4)) Setting too chaotic, for example disaster relief. Treatment assigned at too high a level, for example national policy.



04

Maybe not worth it for learning
The answer is already known from credible existing studies, or there is no generalizable “why” because the programme is one-off with little scale or replication potential.



If an RCT is the right tool in principle, Step 4 checks whether it is feasible in practice: oversubscription, timing, legal basis, institutional buy-in and measurable outcomes.

title: Step 1: develop a Theory of Change
text:
Step 1›Step 2›Step 3›Step 4›Step 5›Step 6›Step 7
Before any data is collected and before any evaluation contract is signed, a Managing Authority needs to be clear about what the programme is trying to achieve, how progress toward that goal will be measured, and what data will be needed to do so. A ToC makes this logic explicit and evaluation-ready.
crumbs: Step 1: develop a Theory of Change

title: Step 1: develop a Theory of Change
text:
Define a ToC

What is a ToC - and how does it relate to your intervention logic?
Managing Authorities preparing ERDF or ESF+ programmes are already required to articulate an intervention logic - a structured account of how a policy instrument is expected to produce its intended results. A ToC builds on this familiar concept and makes it more explicit and evaluation-ready.
Where an intervention logic maps the pathway from inputs to outputs to results, a ToC adds two important elements: it specifies the assumptions that must hold at each step for the logic to work, and it makes clear which links in the chain are strong and which are uncertain. This is precisely the information an randomised controlled trials (RCT) is designed to test.
If your programme already has a well-developed intervention logic in its programme document or partnership agreement, you have a strong starting point. The task of building a ToC is largely one of making that logic more precise - defining each step clearly enough that it can be measured.


Components of a ToC
A ToC follows a causal chain from resources invested to long-term change achieved, with assumptions sitting at every junction:


  
    
      
    
  

  
  
  
  
  
  

  
  
  INPUTS

  
  ACTIVITIES

  
  OUTPUTS

  
  SHORT-TERM
  OUTCOMES

  
  MEDIUM-TERM
  OUTCOMES

  
  GOALS

  
  
  Assumption

  
  Assumption

  
  Assumption

  
  Assumption

  
  Assumption

Assumptions sit at every transition in the causal chain and must hold for the logic to work.

Inputs are the resources, efforts, and actions invested in a policy. For ERDF programmes, inputs typically include ERDF co-financing, national co-financing, and the administrative capacity of the Managing Authority and intermediate bodies.

North-East Romania: inputs

Number of staff involved in designing and implementing the digitalisation grants
Available budget to disrupt digitalisation grants


Activities are the concrete actions undertaken to deliver the programme. These are what the programme actually does.

North-East Romania: activities

Outreach and information campaign for potential applicants
Pre-assessment questionnaire to express interest in digitalization grants
Call for proposals to deliver digitalisation grants


Outputs are represent the direct and immediate results of the activities conducted within a policy. They are tangible and observable products or deliverables that demonstrate the completion of specific tasks. For ERDF programmes, these correspond closely to the common output indicators that Managing Authorities are already required to report to the European Commission.

North-East Romania: outputs

Digitalisation grants are awared to selected companies


Short-term outcomes refer to the immediate changes that occur as a direct result of the outputs. These outcomes are often related to changes in knowledge, attitudes, skills, and behaviors among the target population. Although short-term outcomes are not the program’s ultimate goals, they play a crucial role in achieving the larger objectives.

North-East Romania: short-term outcomes

Digital solution procured, installed, configured and tested
Digital solution is operationalized, used by employees, customers and others in the supply chain.​​


Medium-term outcomes are the intermediate changes that occur due to sustained efforts and progress from short-term outcomes. These outcomes indicate progress toward the overall goal and often involve shifts in social norms, policies, or organizational practices. These correspond closely to the common result indicators that ERDF and ESF+ programmes report on, though impact evaluations typically aim to go further by establishing a credible causal link between the programme and the result.

North-East Romania: preregister the evaluation design

Companies achieve advanced digital transformation
Improved time management and business efficiency


Goals are a policy’s broad, long-term aspirations or objectives. They describe the ultimate impact or change that the policy aims to achieve. Goals are usually overarching and may require significant time and effort to accomplish.

North-East Romania: goals

Increase in sales, employment, productivity (TFP) and profitability
Higher resilience to economic shocks, due to the business versatility ensured though the digital solutions


Assumptions are the underlying beliefs, conditions, or factors that are considered to be true but have not yet been fully proven or tested. Assumptions may involve external factors, stakeholder behavior, or contextual influences that must align for the theory to work as expected.

North-East Romania: assumptions

Employees will possess, or will be able to acquire, the digital skills needed to effectively use the solution for advanced digital transformation
Companies have sufficient organizational flexibility to change internal processes
Companies have the organizational capacity
Companies’ customers and suppliers are sufficiently active in digital channels (online payments, e-commerce transactions, digital invoicing) to make adoption beneficial
Suppliers, partners, and customers will engage with and utilize digital links (communications, transactions, data exchange) established by companies, ensuring network effects and value creation.




Why invest time in developing a ToC?
Developing a ToC is well worth the effort for two important reasons. First, it sharpens the design of your evaluation. By mapping out the causal logic of an intervention, a ToC generates clear research questions and helps teams identify which outcomes to measure and what data to collect. It can be built collaboratively – by starting from the desired final outcomes and working backwards through the chain of events needed to get there – and this process is particularly useful in a programme partnership context, where multiple stakeholders may have different views on how the policy is supposed to work. It also prompts a credibility check: is there actually evidence, from comparable programmes in other regions or member states, to support each step in the logic?
Second, a ToC produces richer and more transferable policy lessons. Measuring the right intermediate outcomes reveals not just whether an intervention worked, but how and why it worked. Opening this “black box” transforms evaluation results from a simple pass/fail verdict into actionable insight that can inform the next programming period. The knowledge gained also travels better – findings grounded in a clear causal logic are more readily applied by other Managing Authorities facing similar challenges in different regional contexts.

North-East Romania: why investing time
In Romania, the World Bank supported the Managing Authority in developing a ToC and in applying systematic methods to quantify the Managing Authority’s own expectations about programme impacts before the call launched. This exercise revealed gaps between what the programme was designed to achieve and what its indicators actually measured – allowing the design to be adjusted before implementation rather than after the evaluation.

By this point you have mapped your programme’s causal logic, defined what you want to find out, and chosen the indicators you will use to measure it. The question this step answers is whether you can actually run a randomised evaluation to get those answers - and if so, how to design it.
A randomised controlled trial (RCT) is not always possible. Before investing time and resources in a randomised design, a Managing Authority needs to check whether the basic conditions are in place. Once they are, the choice of randomisation method matters: different programme shapes call for different designs. This page covers both.

title: Step 4: assess feasibility of conducting an RCT
section: Five conditions for a feasible RCT
text:
Five conditions for a feasible RCT
Work through these five questions before committing to a randomised design. If the answer to the first three is not yes, an RCT is unlikely to be feasible and you should explore alternative approaches with your evaluation team.


1. Is the programme oversubscribed?
An RCT requires more eligible applicants than available funding slots. If you can support everyone who qualifies, there is no basis for a lottery – and no credible comparison group. Oversubscription is the single most important precondition.


2. Is there enough time?
Randomisation must happen before the first grant is awarded. If the programme has already launched, it is too late. Planning must ideally begin at the programme design stage.


3. Is there a legal basis?
Most national frameworks were designed around ranking or first-come-first-served selection and say nothing about random assignment. Explicit permission – either in existing regulations or through a programme-specific instrument – must be confirmed before proceeding.


4. Is there political and institutional buy-in?
An RCT requires sustained commitment from the Managing Authority and any intermediate bodies involved in delivery. If key stakeholders are not on board, or if political changes could interrupt the evaluation midway, the investment may not be recoverable.


5. Can the outcomes actually be measured?
The indicators selected in Step 3 must be observable – through administrative records, a survey, or both. If the primary outcome cannot be reliably measured for both treatment and comparison firms, the evaluation will not produce credible results even if the design is sound.



Is randomisation permitted under your national legal framework?
Before designing the lottery or scoring mechanism, confirm that your national legal framework – and the specific legislation governing your programme – either explicitly permits randomisation as a selection method or is flexible enough to accommodate it.
Most national frameworks were designed around ranking or first-come-first-served selection and say nothing about random assignment. A clear legal basis is the precondition for experimental evaluation to happen at all. See the legal framework page for country examples, key legal elements, and practical steps →**

title: Step 4: assess feasibility of conducting an RCT
text:
Do you have enough firms?
To detect the impact of a programme, you need enough firms in both the treatment and comparison groups. Too few firms and even a real effect may be invisible – ordinary variation between firms drowns out the signal. The technical term for this is statistical power, but the practical question is simple: is your eligible pool large enough?

title: Step 4: assess feasibility of conducting an RCT
section: Lesson 1: link eligibility directly to programme objectives
text:
Lesson 1: link eligibility directly to programme objectives
Vague or broadly defined eligibility criteria are one of the most common weaknesses in EU-funded programmes. When eligibility is not tightly linked to the programme’s Theory of Change, three problems tend to follow: the wrong firms enter the pool, evaluators cannot assess applications consistently, and the evaluation cannot cleanly measure whether the programme reached its intended beneficiaries.
Eligibility criteria should be specific enough to identify firms with the highest potential to benefit, while remaining broad enough – where there is genuine uncertainty about who will benefit – to allow equal opportunities across the potential target population. Criteria should also be measurable: if an evaluator cannot determine objectively whether a firm meets a criterion, neither can the firm.

Spain
In Spain, the World Bank found that eligibility criteria for an innovation support programme included vague language – such as references to the “incentive effect of aid” – that was open to arbitrary interpretation by evaluators. The World Bank worked with the Managing Authority to rewrite the criteria, develop a structured scoring rubric aligned with the programme’s Theory of Change, and standardise the evaluation panel process. The result was a more transparent selection process that was easier for firms to understand and for evaluators to apply consistently.
crumbs: Step 4: assess feasibility of conducting an RCT

title: Step 4: assess feasibility of conducting an RCT
section: Lesson 2: Base programme design on evidence of need
text:
Lesson 2: Base programme design on evidence of need
Programmes that are designed without a prior assessment of beneficiary needs frequently suffer from misalignment: either too few firms apply (under-subscription), or the programme attracts firms that are not its intended target. Both problems are expensive – leading to repeated calls, unused funds, or support that reaches firms that would have done well without it.
A baseline needs assessment – conducted before the programme launches – allows the Managing Authority to understand the regional landscape, calibrate grant sizes and eligibility thresholds, and anticipate demand more accurately. Where uncertainty about demand remains, piloting different programme elements before full-scale rollout can reduce the risk of costly mismatches.

Italy
In Italy, a minibond programme pre-identified 289 eligible firms, of which only 30 applied – a hit rate of 10.3%. Of the 19 firms that ultimately issued a minibond, most had access to alternative financing and may not have needed the programme at all. A prior needs assessment could have revealed that the programme’s terms were less attractive than alternative instruments already available in the region – including zero-interest loans and non-repayable grants from earlier programmes – and that the design needed to be adjusted accordingly before launch.
crumbs: Step 4: assess feasibility of conducting an RCT

title: Step 4: assess feasibility of conducting an RCT
section: Lesson 3: Set measurable indicators from the start
text:
Lesson 3: Set measurable indicators from the start
Without measurable outcome indicators tied to clear objectives, programmes cannot be held accountable for their results – and evaluations cannot determine whether they worked. Targets are frequently treated as administrative end goals rather than as part of a broader results chain, which means that even well-implemented programmes struggle to demonstrate impact.
A Theory of Change developed before the programme launches provides the framework for identifying which outcomes to measure, at which level of the causal chain, and over what time horizon. Indicators should be specific, observable, and linked to the data sources that will actually be available at the time of measurement.

Romania
In Romania, the World Bank supported the Managing Authority in developing a Theory of Change and in applying systematic methods to quantify the Managing Authority’s own expectations about programme impacts before the call launched. This exercise revealed gaps between what the programme was designed to achieve and what its indicators actually measured – allowing the design to be adjusted before implementation rather than after the evaluation. The process also produced a baseline report on 1,038 MSMEs that passed the eligibility screening, giving the evaluation team the pre-intervention data needed to measure change.
crumbs: Step 4: assess feasibility of conducting an RCT

title: Step 4: assess feasibility of conducting an RCT
section: Lesson 4: Invest heavily in outreach – especially to reach new beneficiaries
text:
Lesson 4: Invest heavily in outreach – especially to reach new beneficiaries
Standard outreach channels – newsletters, social media posts, agency websites – consistently fail to reach the firms that EU programmes are designed to serve. Firms without prior experience of EU funding, smaller firms, and firms in rural or remote areas are systematically less likely to apply, not because they are ineligible but because they do not know the programme exists or lack the resources to navigate the application process.
Effective outreach requires direct, personalised engagement: in-person events, road trips to municipalities, collaboration with mayors and local business associations, and hands-on application support. Experimenting with different outreach approaches – and measuring which ones work – can significantly expand the eligible pool and improve the quality of applications.

North-East Romania: building the eligibility pool
In North-East Romania, the World Bank randomised outreach activities across 46 cities, selecting 26 for road-trips where a consultant explained the call and helped firms complete the pre-assessment survey. Cities that received road-trips produced 110 applications compared to 71 in cities that did not – a 55% increase. Applications from road-trip cities also came from significantly smaller firms (12.6 employees on average, compared to 19.6 in comparison cities). Compared to previous calls, the total number of applicants tripled and the number of eligible firms more than doubled. This small experiment demonstrated both the effectiveness of in-person mobilisation and the value of embedding experimentation into programme implementation.
crumbs: Step 4: assess feasibility of conducting an RCT

title: Step 4: assess feasibility of conducting an RCT
text:
Lesson 5: Simplify the application process
Complex, document-heavy application processes disproportionately burden firms that are least familiar with EU funding – the very firms that programmes are often designed to reach. When compliance requirements are similar regardless of grant size, small firms face the same administrative burden as large ones, often pushing them to hire consultants and creating a market for intermediaries that adds cost without adding value.
Application requirements should be proportionate to the amount of funding requested. Processes should be fully digital, integrated with existing administrative databases wherever possible, and capable of providing real-time eligibility feedback so that firms can assess their likelihood of success before investing significant time in an application.

North-East Romania: building the eligibility pool
In Romania, the pre-assessment survey was designed to do three jobs simultaneously: collect baseline data for the evaluation, assess firm eligibility in real time, and provide firms with enough information to decide whether to proceed – all within approximately 40 minutes. Survey responses were automatically cross-referenced with official firm data, enabling instant verification of core eligibility criteria. Firms that did not meet the requirements were informed immediately, saving them from investing further time in a formal application that would have been rejected. Eligible firms received individualised benchmark reports comparing their digitalization levels to similar firms in their region, providing added value to participants regardless of their eventual selection outcome.
crumbs: Step 4: assess feasibility of conducting an RCT

title: Step 4: assess feasibility of conducting an RCT
section: Lesson 6: Use the application process to exchange information
text:
Lesson 6: Use the application process to exchange information
The application process is typically treated as a one-way flow of information: firms submit data to the Managing Authority. In practice, it can also be a vehicle for delivering useful information and tools to firms – raising awareness about a topic (digitalization, innovation, energy efficiency), helping firms identify investment needs, and providing benchmarks that inform business decisions regardless of whether the firm is selected for support.
Firms that receive useful information during the application process are more engaged, better prepared to make investment decisions if selected, and more likely to view the experience positively even if they are not funded.

North-East Romania: building the eligibility pool
In the Scinergy pilot in Croatia, the World Bank supported an extensive outreach and information campaign that included a dedicated project website, a LinkedIn campaign with paid promotions, appearances in television and online media, presentations at industry events and scientific institutions, and webinars targeting thousands of firms. The campaign was structured around a business-science matchmaking concept, providing firms with substantive information about how to collaborate with research institutions – not just how to apply for a grant. The initiative attracted widespread media coverage and generated strong interest in applications well before the call officially opened.
crumbs: Step 4: assess feasibility of conducting an RCT

title: Step 4: assess feasibility of conducting an RCT
text:
Lesson 7: Provide early investment guidance
Firms often do not know what to invest in – particularly when the programme targets an unfamiliar area such as digitalization, R&D collaboration, or energy efficiency. Left without guidance, firms make poorly informed investment choices, which reduces the quality of applications and the eventual impact of the programme. Early, impartial guidance reduces this risk and shifts part of the technical burden away from the Managing Authority.
Investment guidance can take the form of general information materials distributed at the programme’s launch, templates that help firms assess their needs, or structured engagement with expert advisors (such as Digital Innovation Hubs). Conflicts of interest must be managed carefully if advisors also provide services to applicants.

North-East Romania: building the eligibility pool
In the North-East digitalization programme, the Managing Authority required applicants to produce a digital feasibility study prepared and signed by a certified digital expert – either from a European Digital Innovation Hub or an ICT consulting firm. A standardised template guided firms through assessing their current digital maturity (using the DESI framework), identifying areas for improvement, and specifying the technologies they planned to invest in. This shifted the technical evaluation away from the agency – which was implementing such a programme for the first time – and toward independent experts, while ensuring that investment proposals were grounded in an objective assessment of each firm’s starting point.

The answer depends on how large an effect you expect, how much firms vary on the outcome of interest, and how confident you want to be in the result. An evaluator will run a power calculation to translate these inputs into a minimum required sample. More details on power calculations →
If the eligible pool falls short, there are two immediate levers:


Loosen the eligibility bar
If fewer firms qualify than needed, lowering the eligibility threshold adds more firms to the pool you randomise from. Be careful not to dilute the target population so much that the evaluation no longer answers the original question.


Widen the ranking bands
If you are scoring applicants, avoid treating small score differences as decisive. Group firms with similar scores into bands and treat everyone in a band as equally eligible – this moves more firms into the randomised pool rather than having marginal cases decided by a single point.

title: Step 4: assess feasibility of conducting an RCT
section: Five ways to randomise your programme
text:
Five ways to randomise your programme
Not every programme fits the same shape. The right design depends on your programme’s structure, budget, and the learning questions you would like to answer. Here are five approaches in common use.

  
    Lottery
    How: randomly select which eligible firms receive the programme, by a documented public or private draw.
    Best when: eligibility is clear, the programme is oversubscribed, and a single treatment is being tested.
  
  
    Multiple treatment arms
    How: randomly assign firms to different versions of the programme — for example, grant only vs. grant plus advisory support — with or without a comparison group receiving nothing.
    Best when: you want to know which design element drives results, not just whether the programme works at all.
  
  
    Randomised phase-in
    How: everyone receives the programme eventually, but in a randomly assigned order. Firms still waiting serve as the comparison group in the meantime.
    Best when: budget or capacity limits mean you cannot reach all eligible firms at once, and withholding support permanently would be unacceptable.
  
  
    Randomised intensities
    How: vary the dose of the programme across firms — for example, 100%, 50%, or 0% of eligible employees receive training.
    Best when: you suspect that knowledge or behaviour spreads between treated and untreated workers within the same firm, and you want to measure that spread.
  
  
    Encouragement design
    How: randomise who receives extra outreach or information encouraging take-up, rather than randomising access to the programme itself.
    Best when: the programme cannot legally be denied to anyone who qualifies — for example, an open voucher scheme — but take-up is voluntary and varies.
  


North-East Romania used a lottery
North-East Romania used a simple lottery. The 1,038 eligible firms were split into two equal groups of 519 by a random draw. The treatment group was invited to apply for a grant of between €15,000 and €100,000 to invest in equipment, software, or services. The firms in the comparison group were not invited to apply and thus, received no grant. Both groups were surveyed in the same way throughout the evaluation period.

title: Step 4: assess feasibility of conducting an RCT
text:
Public or private lottery?
Once you have decided to use a lottery, a second design choice arises: should the draw be conducted publicly or behind the scenes?



Public lottery


The draw takes place in front of an audience – for example, pulling firm names from a hat at a public event, or livestreaming the computerised draw.
Advantage: maximises transparency and public trust. Firms can see for themselves that the process was fair.
Disadvantage: once comparison firms know they did not receive support, they may change their behaviour – working harder to find alternative funding, for example – which can reduce the measured difference between the groups.




Private lottery


The draw is conducted internally by the evaluation team, with full documentation but without public observation.
Advantage: comparison firms do not immediately know the outcome, which reduces the risk of behavioural reactions that narrow the gap between groups.
Disadvantage: the process is less visibly fair, which can make it harder to defend if challenged.




In practice, most RCT evaluations run the draw as a secure, documented, computerised procedure with a verifiable audit trail – combining the rigour of a private draw with the accountability of one that can be independently checked afterwards.

title: Step 4: assess feasibility of conducting an RCT
section: Randomising only part of the pool: a lottery around a cutoff
text:
Randomising only part of the pool: a lottery around a cutoff
In some programmes, it is not practical or desirable to randomise the entire eligible pool. A common alternative is to score all applicants on eligibility criteria, fund the top scorers outright, reject the clear non-qualifiers outright, and randomise only the firms in the middle – those whose scores are close enough together that the difference is not meaningful.
This approach reduces the pool that is randomised, focuses the evaluation on the firms where the decision is genuinely uncertain, and is easier to justify publicly than a lottery across the full range of applicants.

section: Testing programme versions: multiple treatment arms
text:
Testing programme versions: multiple treatment arms
A standard RCT compares one version of the programme against a comparison group. But sometimes the real question is not whether the programme works, but which design works best – grant only versus grant plus mentoring, for example, or light-touch advisory versus intensive coaching.
Multiple treatment arms allow you to test these versions against each other and against a comparison group in a single evaluation. Each group of firms is randomly assigned to a different version, and outcomes are compared across all groups at endline.
The trade-off is sample size: more arms means more groups, and the available pool must be large enough to power comparisons between each pair.

text:
When you cannot fund everyone at once: randomised phase-in
In many programmes, budget or implementation capacity means it is not possible to reach all eligible firms in a single wave. A randomised phase-in turns this constraint into an advantage: firms are randomly assigned to waves, and those still waiting to receive the programme serve as the comparison group for the firms already being treated.
The key advantage is that everyone eventually receives support, which makes the approach easier to justify politically and ethically. The key limitation is that there is no comparison group once the last wave has been treated, which means long-term impacts – those that take several years to emerge – cannot be measured.

Rather than randomising which firms receive the programme, you can randomise how much of it they receive. For example, some firms might have all eligible employees participate in a training programme, while others have only half, and others none. Comparing outcomes across these groups reveals not just whether the programme works but how much of it is needed – and whether the benefits spill over to employees who were not directly treated.

section: When take-up is low: encouragement design
text:
When take-up is low: encouragement design
Some programmes cannot be denied to anyone who qualifies – an open advisory service or a voucher scheme, for example. In these cases, it is not possible to assign firms to a comparison group that is formally excluded from support. The encouragement design offers an alternative: rather than randomising access, randomise who receives extra outreach, information, or a targeted invitation to use the programme.
Firms who receive the encouragement are then compared with those who do not. Because encouraged firms are more likely to take up the programme than non-encouraged firms, the comparison still produces an estimate of the programme’s effect – even if both groups technically had access.
The main limitation is that the estimate reflects the effect of the encouragement itself as much as the programme. If untargeted outreach – a news story, a social media post – reaches both groups, the comparison is diluted.

Compliance is rarely perfect in either direction: some encouraged firms will never take up the programme, and some non-encouraged firms will find it and engage anyway. The right approach is to compare the whole encouraged group with the whole non-encouraged group, regardless of what individual firms actually did. Your evaluation team will handle this in the analysis.

title: Step 4: assess feasibility of conducting an RCT
text:
What are potential challenges?
Even a well-designed RCT must survive contact with reality. These are the four most common problems – and what can be done about each.
Attrition. Firms drop out between the baseline and the endline – because they closed, relocated, or simply refused to participate in a survey again. If drop-out is higher in one group than the other, the two groups are no longer comparable and the impact estimate may be biased. Prevention is far easier than correction: collect multiple contact details at baseline, keep them updated during the programme, and keep the endline survey as short as possible.
Spillovers. Comparison firms benefit from the programme indirectly – a treated supplier passes on improved products, or a treated neighbour shares what they learned in a training session. When this happens, the gap between the groups narrows and the evaluation underestimates the true effect. Spillovers are most likely in concentrated sectors or geographically tight clusters. Where the risk is high, randomising at a higher level – by region or sector cohort rather than by individual firm – can contain it. If spillovers are anticipated, the RCT can be designed in a manner accounting for them.

South Muntenia: designing for spillovers South Muntenia built spillovers into the design. About 900 applicant SMEs are grouped into roughly 100 geographic or sector clusters. Each cluster is randomly assigned a funding intensity of 0%, 33%, 66% or 100%, and firms within each cluster are then randomly selected for funding up to that share. Comparing funded and unfunded firms within a cluster measures each firm’s own return; comparing clusters with different intensities measures the spillover onto neighbours and competitors. Read the full example.

Low take-up. Some firms assigned to the treatment group never use the support – they decline the grant, fail to meet the conditions, or disengage early. Low take-up dilutes the estimated effect: if only half the treatment group actually received the programme, the impact estimate reflects a half-dose. Monitoring take-up actively during implementation – and understanding why firms do not engage – is essential for interpreting what the evaluation ultimately shows.
Uneven implementation. The programme is delivered inconsistently across firms – some receive more advisory time, faster disbursements, or better quality support than others. This introduces noise into the treatment and makes the evaluation harder to interpret. Clear delivery protocols, regular monitoring, and a close relationship between the Managing Authority and the delivery team reduce this risk.

None of these problems make an RCT impossible – but all of them must be anticipated at the design stage, not discovered after the endline survey.


North-East Romania: the programme did not achieve full take-up
Of the 519 firms selected by lottery, only 393 (75.7%) went on to submit a full funding proposal, and 333 (64.2%) were eventually contracted.
Because of limited take-up, it is safer to report the intention-to-treat effect, comparing everyone as originally assigned, even though it understates the effect on the firms that actually took up the grant.

title: More details on comparability of groups
text:
This page explains what balance means, why it matters, how to check it, and what to do if the groups turn out not to be comparable after the lottery.
A randomised lottery is designed to produce two groups – treatment and comparison – that look alike before the programme starts. This comparability is the foundation on which the entire evaluation rests. If the groups are similar at baseline, any difference in outcomes at endline can be attributed to the programme. If they are not, that attribution falls apart.
This page explains what balance means in practice, how to verify it, and – because no lottery produces perfect balance every time – what to do when the groups turn out to be different on some characteristic.

More details on comparability of groups

title: More details on comparability of groups
text:
Why comparability matters so much
The logic of an RCT is simple: take two groups of similar firms, give one group the programme and withhold it from the other, then compare outcomes. The comparison is only meaningful if the two groups were genuinely similar to begin with. If the treatment group happened to contain more high-performing firms before the programme started, any difference in outcomes at endline may simply reflect that head start rather than the programme’s effect.
Randomisation is the mechanism that makes comparability likely – but it does not guarantee it, especially with smaller samples. A random draw can, by chance, produce a treatment group that is slightly older, larger, or more export-oriented than the comparison group. With enough firms, these chance differences average out. With fewer firms, they can be large enough to matter.
This is why the balance check is one of the first things an evaluator does after the baseline survey is complete. It is not a formality – it is a quality control on the randomisation itself.

title: More details on comparability of groups
text:
What a balance check involves
A balance check compares the two groups on a set of characteristics measured at baseline – before the programme has begun and before either group knows whether they have been selected. For firm-level evaluations, these characteristics typically include:

Firm size (number of employees, in full-time equivalents)
Firm age (years since establishment)
Revenue or turnover
Sector or industry classification
Prior R&D or innovation activity
Export participation
The primary outcome variable itself, measured before the intervention

For each characteristic, the evaluator calculates the average value in the treatment group and the average value in the comparison group, and tests whether the difference between them is larger than you would expect by chance from a random draw.

title: More details on comparability of groups
text:
How to read the results
The evaluator will present the balance check as a table showing the average value of each characteristic in each group, the difference between them, and a statistical test of whether that difference is larger than chance would produce. The result of that test is usually expressed as a p-value.



What the result typically shows


In a well-executed randomisation with a reasonably large sample, most characteristics will show no statistically significant difference between the groups. The few that do are usually the result of chance – out of twenty variables tested, you would expect one to appear imbalanced simply because of how probability works, even in a perfectly conducted lottery.




What raises a concern


A concern arises when many variables show imbalance simultaneously, or when the primary outcome variable itself is significantly different at baseline. This suggests the randomisation may have been compromised – perhaps because some firms were selectively excluded, or because the draw was not conducted as described.




One or two imbalanced variables in a balance table is almost always chance. Many imbalanced variables – or imbalance on the primary outcome – is a signal worth investigating.

title: More details on comparability of groups
section: What to do if the groups are not perfectly balanced
text:
What to do if the groups are not perfectly balanced
Perfect balance is the goal, not a guarantee. When the balance check reveals a meaningful difference on one or more characteristics, there are two main responses – and importantly, neither involves re-running the lottery.
Control for the imbalanced variable in the analysis. The most common and appropriate response is to include the imbalanced characteristic as a control variable in the statistical model used to estimate the programme’s impact. This adjusts the comparison to account for the pre-existing difference, producing a more accurate estimate of the programme’s effect. The evaluator handles this – the Managing Authority simply needs to know that it is standard practice, not a workaround.
Do not re-randomise. Once firms know their assignment – or once the programme has begun – re-running the lottery is not an option. It would undermine the integrity of the design and the trust of participants. If a significant imbalance is discovered before the programme launches and before firms have been notified, the evaluation team should be consulted immediately. In rare cases, a new draw may be possible, but this is the exception.

Never drop firms from the analysis because they appear to be outliers or because their inclusion makes the results less clean. Dropping firms selectively – even for apparently good reasons – can introduce bias and undermines the integrity of the evaluation.

title: More details on comparability of groups
section: Choosing what to measure before the lottery – not after
text:
Choosing what to measure before the lottery – not after
The balance check is only part of a broader discipline that runs through every well-designed RCT: deciding what you are going to measure, and how you are going to analyse it, before you see any results.
This applies equally to the outcome variables. The evaluation questions were defined in Step 2, and the indicators were selected in Step 3 – both before the lottery, before the baseline survey, and certainly before any endline data is collected. The reason is simple: if an evaluator can choose which outcome to focus on after seeing the data, they will – consciously or not – tend to report the outcomes that look best. This is called cherry-picking, and it produces findings that appear more favourable or more significant than they actually are.
Pre-registration solves this problem. By publicly committing to the primary outcome, the analysis plan, and the subgroup comparisons before any data is collected, the evaluation team makes it impossible to selectively report results after the fact. The pre-registration record is publicly visible and time-stamped, so anyone reading the final report can verify that the analysis was conducted as originally planned.

Fix the outcomes before the draw: choosing them afterwards invites cherry-picking – even when no one intends it.

section: Pre-registration: locking in the plan publicly
text:
Pre-registration: locking in the plan publicly
Pre-registration means publishing the evaluation design – the research question, the primary outcome, the randomisation procedure, and the analysis plan – on a public registry before data collection begins. It is now a standard requirement for rigorous evaluations and is increasingly expected by academic journals, the European Commission, and research funders.
For a Managing Authority, pre-registration serves two practical purposes beyond scientific integrity. First, it protects the evaluation team from pressure – whether internal or political – to adjust the analysis after results are known. Second, it strengthens the credibility of the findings: when a null result or an inconvenient finding is published, pre-registration demonstrates that it reflects reality rather than selective reporting.


AEA RCT Registry
The most widely used registry for economic and policy evaluations. Free to register. socialscienceregistry.org →


Open Science Framework
Broader registry covering multiple disciplines; supports both pre-registration and open data publication. osf.io/prereg →


RIDIE
Registry for International Development Impact Evaluations, hosted by 3ie. ridie.3ieimpact.org →


Pre-registration should happen before the baseline survey is fielded – or at the very latest, before the endline data is collected. The evaluation team will lead this process, but the Managing Authority should confirm that it has been done before approving the inception report.

With the Theory of Change, evaluation questions, and indicators in place, and the feasibility of the RCT confirmed, the next question is where the data will come from. This is a strategic decision that must be made before the programme launches – not an operational detail to be worked out later. Getting it wrong wastes resources, delays the evaluation, or produces data that cannot support the intended analysis.

title: Step 5: identify available data sources
section: The fundamental decision: primary, secondary, or both?
text:
The fundamental decision: primary, secondary, or both?
For each indicator in your evaluation framework, you must decide whether to rely on primary data collected specifically for the evaluation, secondary data that already exists in administrative records, or a combination of both.
Primary data is information collected directly from target respondents – firms, individuals, or organisations – through surveys or interviews. It gives you control over exactly what is measured and can capture outcomes and mechanisms that administrative records do not contain. The trade-off is cost, time, and respondent burden.
Secondary data draws on records that already exist – national business registries, tax authority data, customs records, patent office databases, or the programme’s own management information system. It is generally cheaper, covers larger samples, and often provides years of pre-intervention history that is invaluable for establishing baselines. The trade-off is that it may not contain the specific variables you need, and access can take time to negotiate.
In countries where administrative data sources – such as business registries, tax records, and social security data – are well established and reliable, as is generally the case across the EU, combining both sources is often the most effective approach: secondary data provides broad coverage and pre-intervention history, while primary survey data captures the outcomes and mechanisms that administrative records cannot.

North-East Romania used a combination of primary and secondary data: self-reported survey data was collected using a structured questionnaire that complements administrative data sources.

title: Step 5: identify available data sources
text:
Assess what you already have
Before commissioning a new survey, take stock of the administrative data you already hold or can access. Programme management systems typically record beneficiary characteristics, grant amounts, payment dates, and reported output indicators. National statistical offices, tax authorities, business registries, and customs agencies hold firm-level data on turnover, employment, exports, costs, expenditures and tax payments – often going back many years, which is particularly valuable for establishing pre-intervention baselines.
Two questions determine whether administrative sources can be useful for an evaluation.
First, do they contain the right outcomes? Administrative records capture variables that may or may not align with the outcomes the evaluation is designed to measure. An innovation programme that wants to measure R&D expenditure or product novelty will find that some business registries simply do not record these. Before relying on administrative data, map each indicator in your evaluation framework against what each source actually contains, and identify the gaps.
Second, can the administrative data be linked to the companies being part of the evaluation? If a firm’s VAT number or national registration number is collected at application stage, it can serve as a linking key to match programme records against tax, registry, or customs data – enabling outcome measurement without any additional burden on firms. Where no common identifier exists, linkage may still be possible through name and address matching, but this requires more effort and introduces matching errors.

text:
Data-sharing agreements
Access to administrative data rarely happens automatically. Tax records, social security data, and business registry microdata are typically held by separate government bodies and subject to their own access rules. Negotiating access takes time – in some countries, many months – and must be initiated well before the evaluation begins.
A data-sharing agreement (DSA) between the Managing Authority and the data-holding body should specify: what data will be shared; in what format and at what level of disaggregation; under what conditions it may be used; who is responsible for data security; and how long it will be retained. GDPR compliance must be addressed explicitly in the agreement.

What comes next

Step 6 covers how to design and field a primary survey – choosing a collection method, designing the questionnaire, selecting respondents, and timing the rounds correctly.

title: Terms of reference for evaluation and data collection
text:
Managing Authorities bring deep knowledge of their programmes to the table; the technical expertise needed to evaluate them rigorously can be contracted in. While this homepage provides the tools and guidance to get started, implementing randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comes with many specificities and challenges – and having the right expert team on board makes all the difference. What Managing Authorities need is a well-crafted Terms of Reference (ToR): the document that attracts the right teams, sets the methodological bar, and defines the conditions for a credible, policy-relevant evaluation. A strong ToR is therefore not a procurement formality – it is the Managing Authority’s most important contribution to the quality of the evaluation.
In principle, a ToR can cover the entire evaluation – including evaluation design, Theory of Change development, and selection of the methodological approach – leaving these decisions to the consultant. However, since this website focuses specifically on RCTs as the evaluation design of choice, it is assumed that Managing Authorities have already completed the preparatory steps covered on the previous pages: the Theory of Change (ToC) is in place, the evaluation questions are defined, the indicators are determined, the feasibility of an RCT has been confirmed, and the available data sources have been mapped. The ToR therefore focuses on two specific functions: preparing and implementing data collection, and conducting the statistical analysis. These can be covered by a single ToR commissioning one consultant or team, or split across two separate ToRs – one for an evaluation consultant responsible for analysis, and one for the data collection firm responsible for fieldwork.

title: Terms of reference for evaluation and data collection
text:
Part 1: the procurement process

Step 1: issue an EoI
For technically complex evaluations, it is strongly recommended to begin with an EoI rather than going directly to a full ToR. An EoI is a short, non-binding call that invites qualified organisations to signal their interest and demonstrate their eligibility before the full competition begins.
The EoI serves three purposes. First, it maps the market – the pool of RCT-capable evaluation teams is narrower than the general consulting market, and an EoI quickly identifies who is actually available and qualified. Second, it allows the Managing Authority to shortlist candidates who are then invited to submit full proposals in a restricted procedure, which is more efficient for both sides. Third, EoI responses often reveal market realities – realistic timelines, typical costs, data access constraints – that can be incorporated into the final ToR.
An EoI should contain:

A brief description of the programme and the intended evaluation approach
The estimated budget range and timeline
Shortlisting criteria: relevant experience, team qualifications, organisational capacity
What to submit: a short letter (maximum 3–5 pages), CVs of key staff, two to three examples of comparable prior evaluations
Submission deadline and contact point

The EoI should be open for a minimum of two to three weeks and published through the national procurement portal and the Managing Authority’s website. Shortlisted candidates – typically three to six – are then invited to submit full proposals in response to the complete ToR.


Step 2: issue the ToR and evaluate proposals
With shortlisted candidates identified, the Managing Authority issues the full ToR. Proposals are evaluated against pre-defined, published criteria. For an RCT evaluation, technical quality should be weighted heavily:



Criterion
Suggested weight




Technical approach and methodology
40%


Relevant experience and past performance
25%


Team qualifications
20%


Price
15%



A low-bid selection for a technically complex evaluation is a false economy. The proposal panel should include at least one member with methodological knowledge of RCTs – or an external technical reviewer where this expertise is not available internally.
Before making a final selection, shortlisted candidates should be invited to a clarification interview. Useful questions include: how would you handle lower-than-projected take-up? At what level of attrition would you consider the evaluation compromised?


Step 3: contract signature and inception
Once the contract is signed, the evaluation begins. The first milestone is the inception report, in which the consultant refines the ToC, finalises the evaluation design, confirms the sampling and randomisation strategy, and presents survey instruments for review. This is the last point at which fundamental design decisions can be changed without significant cost or delay.
Key questions to assess at inception review:

Is the power analysis based on realistic assumptions about take-up, response rates, and effect sizes?
Is the randomisation strategy robust to the specific implementation context?
Has the evaluation been – or is it about to be – pre-registered?
Are all data access arrangements confirmed?

section: Part 2: what the ToR must contain
text:
Part 2: what the ToR must contain

1. Background, programme description, and ToC
This section gives the consultant the context needed to design the data collection instruments and analysis plan. Include:

Name and objectives of the programme and funding instrument

Eligibility criteria and selection methodology

Include the completed ToC, covering inputs, activities, outputs, short- and medium-term outcomes, goals, and assumptions. The ToC has been developed by the Managing Authority and is provided to the consultant as a fixed reference point for designing the measurement framework and survey instruments.


2. Learning questions
List the primary and secondary learning questions explicitly. These have been defined by the Managing Authority and are provided to the consultant as the analytical framework that the data collection and analysis must address. State the intended use of the findings.


3. Scope of work
The consultant’s responsibilities cover two functions: data collection and analysis. Specify clearly which tasks fall under each, and – where a separate data collection firm is contracted – which tasks are covered elsewhere.
Data collection:

Finalise baseline and endline survey instruments based on the ToC and evaluation questions provided
Pilot the questionnaire and propose revisions
Oversee or coordinate fieldwork; supervise the data collection firm where one is separately contracted
Implement randomisation and produce a balance report confirming comparability of treatment and control groups
Design and maintain a monitoring framework tracking take-up, compliance, contamination, and attrition

Analysis:

Clean and merge survey and administrative data
Conduct impact analysis and heterogeneity analysis
Produce draft and final evaluation reports and a non-technical documents (e.g. a policy brief)
Present findings to the Managing Authority and relevant stakeholders



4. Methodology
The methodology section is the technical core of the ToR. It should specify the evaluation design clearly enough that a qualified evaluator can assess whether the approach is appropriate, without being so prescriptive that it prevents the consultant from bringing their own expertise to bear.
Design: Specify that the evaluation will use an RCT, and define the unit of randomisation (typically the firm), the level of randomisation (individual or cluster), and whether there are multiple treatment arms.
Sample size and power: Require a formal power analysis during the inception phase. The consultant must specify and justify the minimum detectable effect, required statistical power, significance level , expected take-up and attrition rates, and baseline variance of the primary outcome.
Estimation: Specify intention-to-treat (ITT) as the primary estimand. Where take-up is imperfect, require the Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE) to be reported alongside ITT. All primary estimates should control for baseline outcome values.
Pre-registration: Require pre-registration on a recognised public registry – such as the AEA RCT Registry – before any data is collected. The pre-registration record must include the research question, randomisation procedure, primary and secondary outcomes, and analysis plan.
Data sources: Specify which administrative datasets will be provided by the Managing Authority and which the consultant must access independently. If primary survey data is needed, clarify whether survey fieldwork is in scope or covered by a separate data collection contract.

7. Data access and GDPR
Specify which datasets the Managing Authority will provide, in what format and timeline. The ToR must address GDPR compliance – lawful basis for processing, pseudonymisation, data security requirements, and retention obligations – and require a data processing agreement to be signed before any data transfer.


8. Qualifications required
For a full RCT evaluation, require: an advanced degree in economics, statistics, or a related quantitative field; demonstrated experience designing and implementing experimental impact evaluations (with publicly available outputs as evidence); experience with firm-level data; and familiarity with EU Cohesion Policy and state aid rules. Common Mistakes to Avoid

Starting too late. An RCT must be designed before beneficiaries are selected. Procurement should begin at least six to twelve months before the first grant is awarded.
Leaving the design entirely to the consultant. The ToR must include a preliminary Theory of Change and evaluation questions – a consultant who receives no guidance will measure what is easy, not what matters.
Setting an unrealistic budget. A ToR with an insufficient budget envelope will either attract low-quality proposals or result in a scope reduction that compromises the evaluation.

title: Step 7: ensure high-quality data
text:
Step 1›Step 2›Step 3›Step 4›Step 5›Step 6›Step 7
Data quality is not something that can be fixed after the fact. Problems that go undetected during fieldwork – inconsistent answers, enumerator errors, item non-response, or systematic biases in who responds – cannot be fully corrected at the analysis stage. The purpose of this step is to put in place the checks that catch these problems early, while there is still time to act on them.
Quality assurance in a randomised controlled trial (RCT) operates at three levels: before fieldwork begins, during fieldwork, and after data collection is complete. Each level requires different tools and different responsibilities.

title: Step 7: ensure high-quality data
section: Before fieldwork: build quality in from the start
text:
Before fieldwork: build quality in from the start
The most effective quality controls are the ones built into the data collection instrument and process before a single interview takes place.
Programme validation rules into the digital form. Every digital survey should include mandatory fields for key variables, range checks (flagging implausible values such as negative employment or turnover greater than a plausible ceiling), logical consistency checks (for example, R&D expenditure cannot exceed total costs), and skip logic that prevents respondents from reaching questions that do not apply to them. These rules catch errors at the point of entry, before they enter the dataset.
Pilot the questionnaire. As described in Step 6, no questionnaire should go to the field untested. The pilot should specifically assess whether questions produce consistent, interpretable answers – not just whether they are understood. If two respondents from similar firms give very different answers to the same question, the wording may be ambiguous even if both respondents felt they understood it.
Train enumerators thoroughly. For Computer-Assisted Telephone Interviews (CATI) and Computer-Assisted Personal Interviews (CAPI) surveys, enumerator quality is one of the strongest predictors of data quality. Training should cover not only how to administer each question but also how to handle refusals, clarify without leading, and record partial responses. Enumerators should complete mock interviews before fieldwork begins.
Pre-specify the analysis plan. Before any data is collected, the primary outcomes, the estimator, and the subgroup analyses should be publicly pre-registered. This prevents selective reporting – the practice of reporting only the results that look good – and provides a clear audit trail from design to findings. Pre-registration is covered under Step 4, but its data quality implications deserve emphasis here: it disciplines both data collection and analysis.

title: Step 7: ensure high-quality data
section: During fieldwork: monitor in real time
text:
During fieldwork: monitor in real time
Once fieldwork begins, the evaluation team should monitor progress continuously rather than waiting for a complete dataset to arrive.
Track response rates by group. Response rates should be monitored separately for the treatment and control groups throughout fieldwork. If response rates diverge significantly – for example, if control firms are less willing to respond – this is an early warning of differential attrition that can bias results.
Conduct back-checks. A back-check involves re-contacting a random subset of completed interviews – typically 10% – to verify a selection of answers. Significant discrepancies between the original interview and the back-check indicate either enumerator error or data fabrication, both of which require immediate investigation. Back-checks are standard practice in CATI and CAPI surveys and should be a contractual requirement for any data collection firm.
Monitor enumerator performance. Each enumerator’s response patterns should be reviewed regularly for signs of data fabrication: unusually short interview durations, identical or near-identical responses across interviews, or suspiciously high completion rates. Any enumerator showing these patterns should be flagged and their recent interviews back-checked at a higher rate.
Flag implausible values immediately. The survey platform should be configured to generate automatic alerts for out-of-range values or logical inconsistencies. These should be reviewed by the field supervisor within 24 hours and, where possible, resolved by calling the respondent back.

title: Step 7: ensure high-quality data
section: After data collection: clean, document, and validate
text:
After data collection: clean, document, and validate
Once fieldwork is complete, the dataset must be cleaned and validated before analysis begins. This process should be systematic and fully documented so that it can be reproduced and audited.
Check balance between treatment and control groups. The first analytical task after baseline data collection is to verify that randomisation produced comparable treatment and control groups. Run balance checks across all key baseline characteristics including firm size, age, sector, turnover, and the primary outcomes at baseline. A significant imbalance on any of these variables should be investigated: it may indicate a flaw in the randomisation procedure, or it may be a chance occurrence that needs to be controlled for in the analysis.
Document all cleaning decisions. Every decision made during data cleaning – how missing values are handled, how outliers are treated, how variables are recoded – must be recorded in a cleaning log. This log is part of the evaluation’s audit trail and should be shared with the Managing Authority alongside the final dataset.
Validate against external sources. Where possible, key variables from the primary survey should be cross-checked against administrative data. For example, self-reported employment figures can be compared against social security records; self-reported turnover can be compared against VAT declarations. Large discrepancies between survey and administrative data are a signal of measurement error that needs to be understood before it affects the analysis.
Assess and report attrition. Compare the characteristics of firms that completed the endline survey with those that did not. If firms that dropped out differ systematically from those that remained – in size, sector, or baseline outcome levels – attrition is selective and may bias the results. Report attrition rates and the results of these comparisons transparently in the evaluation report, and apply appropriate analytical corrections (such as inverse probability weighting) where differential attrition is detected.

title: Step 7: ensure high-quality data
section: A note on administrative data quality
text:
A note on administrative data quality
The quality assurance steps above apply primarily to primary survey data. Administrative data comes with its own quality challenges that require a different approach.
Before using administrative data as an outcome source, the evaluation team should assess: whether variable definitions have changed over the data period; whether there are systematic gaps in coverage (for example, firms below a VAT registration threshold); whether reporting lags mean that the data will be available in time for the evaluation; and whether the data has been used in comparable evaluations and, if so, what quality issues were encountered.
Where administrative data quality is uncertain, the evaluation should include a validation exercise – comparing a subset of administrative records against survey-reported values from the same firms – before relying on it as the primary outcome source.

title: Topic: technology readiness level
text:
What is the current Technology Readiness Level (TRL) of your firm’s main technology or product under development?
Please select the description that best matches the current state of your technology:

TRL 1 – Basic principles observed: Scientific research has begun; basic properties of the technology have been observed and reported
TRL 2 – Technology concept formulated: Application of the technology has been conceived; no experimental proof yet
TRL 3 – Experimental proof of concept: Active research and development has begun; first laboratory studies completed
TRL 4 – Technology validated in laboratory: The technology has been validated in a laboratory environment
TRL 5 – Technology validated in relevant environment: The technology has been validated in an environment relevant to its intended application (e.g. industrial simulation)
TRL 6 – Technology demonstrated in relevant environment: A prototype or pilot system has been demonstrated in a relevant environment
TRL 7 – System prototype demonstration in operational environment: The prototype is close to the planned operational system and has been demonstrated in an operational environment
TRL 8 – System complete and qualified: The technology has been proven to work in its final form and under expected conditions
TRL 9 – Actual system proven in operational environment: The technology is fully mature and has been proven in its final form through successful operation

What is the target TRL your firm aims to reach for this technology within the next [two / three] years? (Select from the same TRL 1–9 scale above)
A note on TRL for Managing Authorities: The TRL scale was originally developed by NASA and adapted by the European Commission for use across all Horizon Europe and ERDF R&D instruments. TRL 1–3 corresponds to basic and applied research; TRL 4–6 to technology development and validation; TRL 7–9 to demonstration and market deployment. Many EU grant schemes specify a minimum entry TRL (e.g. TRL 4 or above) and a target exit TRL, making TRL advancement a natural primary outcome for R&D support evaluations. Self-reported TRL should ideally be validated against objective evidence (e.g. prototype documentation, test reports) where possible.

text:
Product innovation

Definition: Introduction of a new or significantly improved good or service
Metric: Binary indicator (yes/no); number of new products introduced; share of turnover from new products (%)
Data source: Primary survey (CIS-based questions)


Process innovation

Definition: Introduction of a new or significantly improved production, delivery, or supporting process
Metric: Binary indicator (yes/no); type of process innovation introduced
Data source: Primary survey (CIS-based questions)


Organisational innovation

Definition: Introduction of new organisational methods in business practices, workplace organisation, or external relations
Metric: Binary indicator (yes/no)
Data source: Primary survey


Novelty of innovation

Definition: Whether innovations are new only to the firm, new to the market, or new to the world – a measure of innovation ambition
Metric: Categorical (firm-level / market-level / world-level novelty)
Data source: Primary survey


Share of turnover from new products

Definition: The proportion of sales generated by products or services introduced in the last three years – captures commercial success of innovation
Metric: % of total turnover attributable to new or significantly improved products
Data source: Primary survey


Innovation expenditure

Definition: Total spending on innovation-related activities (R&D, design, training, market introduction, etc.)
Metric: Total innovation expenditure in €; share of turnover spent on innovation (%)
Data source: Primary survey or administrative (tax records with R&D tax credit data)
